utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We have been in recess for three weeks. I suppose we do not have to re-introduce ourselves, do we? We look like the same people! We are here to hear oral arguments on the Defence motion on dismissal of charges. We will hear from the Defence first. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. Wladimiroff, as well as Mr. Niemann, we have carefully read the submissions of the parties and we have read all of the transcripts of witnesses' testimony which is implicated by the motion, so do not just reiterate what is said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. We did trust you would, so I am not going to repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So my point is that we have very carefully looked at the submissions and the transcript and read every word. So we would like to hear from the parties this morning, but we do not want you just to reiterate what is said. You may proceed, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Indeed, instead of repeating arguments expressed in our motion, I rather prefer to address straight ahead the discussion raised by the Prosecution in their response to our motion. Before doing so, I want to emphasise that our motion will not, as the Prosecution suggest, result in a delay of the trial process. On the contrary, I would say that a dismissal of the charges will certainly reduce the number of issues to be tried and reduce the length of 28 the trial, the time spent by all the parties, including the Court, in dealing with those matters during evidence, arguments and deliberations will be reduced. Let me move to the first assertion of the Prosecution, that is, there is no provision in the Statute or the Rules for a no case to answer or no prima facie case submission to be made at the trial or for any type of intermediate consideration of the charges in the case. As a matter of fact, they say that the Rules provide that the Trial Chamber is to receive all possible evidence prior to considering the criminal responsibility of an accused for any charge, and that the only Rule which addresses deliberations, Rule 87, states that the Trial Chamber shall deliberate when both parties have completed their presentation of the case. Let me focus on Rule 87. This Rule actually states: "When both parties have completed their presentation of the case, the Presiding Judge shall declare the hearing closed, and the Trial Chamber shall deliberate in private". The Rule does not state, as it seems in the argument of the Prosecution, that the Trial Chamber may only deliberate after both parties have completed their presentation of the case. It is certainly not the case that Rule 87 bars our motion. The next argument of no provision in the Rules is also invalid. The Rules were not designed to cover every possible detail of court procedures. Where the Rules only deal with basic aspects of the proceedings, a lot is left to the discretion of the Judges. The general provision of Rule 54 is 28 an excellent example of this. Given this character of the Rules, it is not significant that the Rules do not provide specifically for a type of motion as we filed. As a matter of fact, we are in very good company, your Honours. Morris and Sharf state in their textbook, An Inside Guide to the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, page 257, I quote: "Since the burden of the proof is on the prosecution, the defence may want to hear all of the evidence and then decide whether to argue that the prosecution has failed to meet its burden of the proof and make a motion to that effect or to go forward with the defence. There is no provision in the Statute or the Rules expressly authorising the defence to bring a motion to dismiss the charges based on insufficient evidence at the conclusion of the prosecution's case. However, this type of motion may be considered to be included in the general right of the defence to bring a motion for appropriate relief or ruling under Rule 72." It seems to me that your Honours share the same view. Why would you otherwise enquire whether the Defence would consider such a motion as it appears on August 7th, pages 3134 up to 3135? Let me move to the other arguments, that is, the assertion that the motion is unknown in civil law jurisdictions. If we look to the response, we see that with reference to the unique character of the international jurisdiction of the Tribunal and the concomitant requirement to 28 consider principles of the divergent justice systems, the Prosecution also asserts that a motion for dismissal is unknown in civil law jurisdictions. This argument may look right, your Honours, but it is not correct in daily practice. The principle of "burden of the proof" for the Prosecution, of course, also applies in civil law jurisdictions. Under this principle, accused persons in civil law jurisdictions may move for an acquittal during the trial and before its closure. When I, for example, anticipate on the basis of the file in a Dutch case that the Prosecution will not meet the burden of the proof during the trial, I may decide not to call Defence witnesses. I will certainly move for an acquittal after the presentation of insufficient evidence by the Prosecution, and argue that if the Court rejects that motion, the Court should allow the Defence by interlocutory decision to call Defence witnesses. So we can easily do that in our system. But, even assuming that the motion for dismissal is unknown to civil law jurisdictions, this argument is not relevant because the proceedings before this Tribunal are certainly not based on the inquisitorial system of civil law jurisdictions. Part 6 of the Rules dealing with proceedings before the Trial Chamber is, undoubtedly, derived from the Bench Trials of common law jurisdictions. Bassiouni and Manikas write in that textbook, The Law of the International Criminal Tribunal for Former Yugoslavia, at page 863: "The vision of the Tribunal's proceedings, as it 28 emerged from the Secretary General's Report, is clearly that of an adversarial system reflecting the common law tradition. This is markedly different from the traditional Roman-Civilist approach referred to as the inquisitorial system. The Rules enacted further develop the adversarial features of the Tribunal." Where these authors state: "On occasion, however, particular provisions may be found which incorporate elements of contemporary European civilist systems", there is no reason to believe that they had in mind that as a consequence of these elements a motion of dismissal would not be allowed during the trial. I would say, on the contrary, Bassiouni and Manikas emphasise that, "On the whole, the process, procedures and rules evidence developed are clearly marked by the American experience. In fact, many of the Rules may be viewed as counterparts or parallels of US Federal practices." In common law countries the Judge may, at a certain resting place during the trial, be called on to say whether the condition of the evidence is such that the case may be disposed of without running the full course. Juries also may return verdicts of acquittal before a case has concluded, if they consider they have heard enough evidence. Again, following your enquiry about the motion of dismissal on August 7th, it seems to me that your Honours share the view that the filing of such motion is consonant to the adversarial character of part 6 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. 28 Although the Prosecution acknowledge different types of prima facie cases, their main legal argument is that the standard of a prima facie case as it emerged from Rule 47(A) should be applied to determine our motion. In the development of their argument the Prosecution ignores, however, that Rule 47 is designed for pretrial proceedings and not for proceedings before the Trial Chamber. The purpose of Rule 47 is to provide for a safeguard against unreasonable or unwarranted action on the part of the prosecutor before nailing a person as an accused in public. In a pretrial procedure before a confirming Judge, the test of a prima facie case is limited to written material supplied by the Prosecution to the confirming Judge. That material is not evidence according to section 3 of part 6 of the Rules as it has not been examined, for example, on reliability before a Judge. In this pretrial procedure, the Prosecution does not have the burden of proof as required before the Trial Chamber, but a legal burden before the confirming Judge that the material shown to him points to facts and circumstances that would justify a reasonable and ordinary prudent man to believe that a suspect has committed a crime. Before the Trial Chamber, though, the rules of evidence apply and any information or material brought before the Judges is subject to both cross-examination of either party and questions of the judges. In this context, it is significant that (as in domestic adversarial systems) the sequence of case 28 presentation before the Trial Chamber is that the Prosecution has to start with presentation of evidence. The consequence of the burden of proof in an adversarial criminal proceeding is, therefore, that the Prosecution will have to discharge itself of that burden, regardless of case presentation by the Defence. This implies that the evidence should meet the burden of proof after the conclusion of the Prosecution's case. That burden is met when the Prosecution has established that the Trial Chamber in the absence of other evidence could properly convict the accused. Such a prima facie case has been established when the evidence admitted has reached the standard of Rule 87(A). So the proper standard for this kind of prima facie case is, therefore, proof of guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. Which factors should be taken into account then? If your Honours are going to decide our motion on the basis of the standard of a prima facie case under Rule 47, as the Prosecution suggest, it would certainly not make sense to take into account factors such as the reliability of witnesses, consistency of previous statements with testimony given in Court and the strength of identification evidence, whereas the test of a prima facie case under Rule 47 is limited to information, regardless of its weight as evidence after examination. We trust that will not be the case here. I am confident that your Honours will decide our motion on the basis of the proper standard of a prima facie case under Rule 87 by 28 determining whether, by absence of other evidence, the weight of the evidence submitted is sufficient or not. Weighing the evidence consonant with Rules 89 up to 98 implies that general factors related to reliability, consistency, collaboration and identification should be taken into account, as well as specific factors related to the nature of the conflict. If I now proceed to an analysis of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just ask you a question? What do you mean by "related to the nature of the conflict"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The distinction between an ordinary crime under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Specifically, there was no mention in your motion, nor in the response, regarding whether this is an armed conflict in an international setting or an internal setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not talking about that; are you saying that instead the evidence must show that the acts were committed in the context of an armed conflict as opposed to whether it was international or internal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We did not raise that point in the context of the difference between an ordinary crime and a crime under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. We raised this point as a factor to be taken into account because that could influence the way people express themselves as a witness in court, being a part of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, in your submission you said that the witnesses were all of a different ethnicity and, therefore, had 28 a desire or a motive, I suppose, to perhaps embellish on their testimony at the very least. That is what you are talking about in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was under No. 6 of our motion and that is the reason why I refer to that. Your Honours, the factual comments of the Prosecution to our scrupulous analysis of the evidence are really not inviting for a useful debate. The essence of the response of the Prosecution to our evaluation of the discharge of the evidential burden is more or less dressed up, "Yes, we have", where we have argued, "No, you have not". I do not think that a factual elaboration along the same lines will help your Honours much further. In our motion we have set out in detail and per allegation the contradictory and flawed evidence that has undermined the claim of the Prosecution that all charges will be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Where witnesses gave conflicting accounts, false allegations or tenuous identifications, we have shown that there is no case to answer. Here I would like to cite Cross and Tapper On Evidence, edition 1995 at page 192, where they write: "Questions of the sufficiency of evidence are usually raised on a submission that there is no case to answer. The Judge must rule in favour of the submission if there is insufficient evidence to prove an essential element in the ... 28 case, or if the evidence which has been adducted is so tenuous that no jury properly directed could convict upon it. It is not enough when any weakness in the ... case depends on matters within the exclusive jurisdiction of the jury, such as reliability of witnesses." They also write: "While honesty of a witness should properly remain to be decided by the jury, there are situations, such as identification, where the evidence even of an honest witness might be regarded as tenuous." Another issue ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page in Cross and Tapper?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is page 192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, another issue I would like to elaborate a little bit further is the requirement of corroboration of evidence. Different to common law jurisdictions where one witness is sufficient in all cases, most civil law jurisdictions maintain the unus testis nullus testis rule. Bearing this in mind, it seems significant to me that Rule 96(i) states expresses verbis that "no corroboration of the victim's testimony shall be required" in the context of a rape case. This requirement would not make any sense if corroboration of evidence would not be required at all. A reasonable interpretation a contrario, therefore, is that in other cases the corroboration is indeed required. This interpretation is consistent with Rule 89(B) that stipulates that a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which will best 28 favour a fair examination of matters before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law. In this connection, I would like to mention that the Court heard evidence from one witness only on counts 12, 13 and 14. Talking about the spirit of the Statute and general principles of law, I emphasise that a fundamental tenet of civil law jurisdictions is that in order to amount to corroboration, the evidence has to emanate from a source independent of the witness to be corroborated or, in a still extreme form, from a different type of source from the witness to be corroborated. More in general I note that where the indictment contains a number of similar counts reflecting a succession of different incidents related by common factors, of course each count will have to be considered separately. Citing Cross and Tapper again at page 168 up to 169, I may reflect the opinion of the Court of south Australia in the R. v. Van Beelen case responding to the question if there can be satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt of guilt of the accused when there is no such satisfaction with regard to any of the evidentiary facts. On this, the Court expressed itself as follows: "There is a clear distinction between drawing an inference of guilt from a combination of several proved acts, none of which by itself would support the inference, and drawing an inference of guilt from several facts whose existence is in 28 doubt. In the first place, the combination does what each fact taken in isolation could not do; in the second case the combination counts for nothing. " Finally, I would like to recall that Article 7 of the Statute holds a person responsible, who planned, instigated, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime. The indictment, though, alleges that Tadic participated in the crimes. The Defence takes the position that participation within the criminal responsibility of the Statute requires an active involvement in the execution of a crime. It is not enough to be present whilst a crime is committed, if the accused takes no part in it and does not act in concert with those who commit it, unless he watched for his companions in order to permit the commission of the crime. The evidence does not meet this standard. If I may conclude my arguments, your Honours? The removal of allegations not proven, and the stigma attached, at the earliest possible opportunity is a prime objective of any criminal justice system. The deliberate retention (as the Prosecution wishes) of unsubstantiated allegations that may be removed at an appropriate stage would be a clear breach of Article 7 of the International Covenant, which provision, although not strictly binding, should guide the Trial Chamber in this matter. We trust that the Trial Chamber will find that the allegations as discussed in our motion are indeed 28 unsubstantiated. We request you to dismiss these counts against Dusko Tadic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff, just a few questions: Are you saying that if there are multiple witnesses who testify with respect to a particular count, let us say three witnesses, and if the testimony of one of those witnesses is sufficient to satisfy the elements of the offence as charged in the count, that that testimony alone is not enough to withstand the motion of dismissal of that particular count?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If it is not -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying instead we must have at least two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There should be any form of independent corroboration, that is the argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is true, that is what is required in 96(i), that is for sure, and it requires that there is no corroboration. You, perhaps, could look at it this way, that the specific reference in 96(i) to the requirement of corroboration is an indication that with respect to other crimes there is no requirement of corroboration, otherwise why put that in 96(i)?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is the way you read it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One could read it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I have been referring to 96. Let me go to your reference then. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 96(i) says, "No corroboration of the victim's testimony shall be required". The preceding, though, phrase is 28 "in cases of sexual assault". So there is a premise. I suppose it is recognised by some jurisdictions that if there is a specific reference that something is not required, that specific reference is necessary to indicate that it is not required in that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Exactly what I have been arguing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And it is not required in cases of sexual assault. That is why it is in that particular Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But if it were not required with respect to other crimes that are charged under the Statute, there would have been no need to make this specific reference in cases dealing with sexual assault. Having participated in the drafting of the Rules, I suggest that it is a possible reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I argued was that it is a requirement of the Rules that there should be a corroboration but not in cases of sexual assault.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right. No corroboration in sexual assault.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exactly. That was put in there to make it very clear that in those cases no corroboration should be required. So what I am suggesting is that that may not, therefore, indicate that corroboration is required in other cases, but instead there was a specific focus on this particular type of offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As I argued, it may not have been in the mind of the Judges when they drafted these Rules, but I have been 28 arguing that in civil law jurisdictions you have this Rule.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Of unus testis nullus testis.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does that require more than one witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: More than one witness to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right, and that is the position that we have taken, it is a very stiff position, at least I argued a middle position that there should be any form of corroboration because that could also be read within the Rules, although you may not have thought about it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We may have thought to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, but it is not expressed in the Rules. The Rules leave the matter open.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Again, I refer (and we do not need to extend it) there is this proposition, at least in terms of Statutes, when you draft a Statute, this is not a Statute, this is a Rule, that when the drafters find it necessary to make a specific reference to something, then by implication what they are saying is that it is required here but not in other instances, but we can differ on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we have taken the view that the Tribunal did not draft technical rules on evidence. You made general provisions and a lot to be left for the Judges to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So, within that system it is possible to do what 28 I suggest to you, because it is not in the Rules that there should be a corroboration and it is not in the Rules that there should not be a corroboration, although you expressed it in Rule 96.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is an open question, as a matter of fact. It may have been in your mind, but it is not in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not in the Rules that there is a corroboration. What you have indicated is that with respect to part 6, which governs our trial proceedings, that, according to Bassiouni and a number of writers have said, "This comes from the common law system". Now what you have done is to ask us to look at a civil law system to require that there be more than one witness as to each of -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As to corroboration. Corroboration might be something other than a witness too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is for sure. Then corroboration of each crime charged in the indictment, because you have indicated that is the system in the civil law, that you have told us that part 6 comes from the common law system ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- as indicated by persons who have been so kind as to write about what we intended and what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I know the feeling.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, but in any case I understand your position, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But, anyhow, I may recall that also Bassiouni wrote 28 that there are elements of civil law jurisdictions adopted within the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am suggesting here that within the Rules this element of civil law jurisdiction should be considered, because it is not expressis verbis forbidden. It is not a settled matter. It may have been one of your reasons why you phrased it as you did but, if you read it, it is not a choice here. It is an open question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that, for example, what you are saying is that if nothing is not specifically in the Rules, that does not mean that we, as Judges, cannot import that or make that a requirement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is to your discretion, that is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But I recall the position that you took with respect to the Prosecutor's motion for disclosure of witness statements of the Defence, your main argument, or one of the arguments, was that it is not in the Rules and so, therefore, they are not entitled to it. I thought you were asking us to focus on these Rules -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is a different issue, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is a different issue, that is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely, because we are dealing here with principles. If we just forget about the Rules and we go back to what is at stake here, disclosure provisions should always be in balance with the evidentiary burdens. I mean, in civil procedure, for example, the evidentiary burden is fairly 28 distributed between the parties; in criminal cases, they are not. They are simply all on one side. They are on the burden, it is the burden of the Prosecution. From that principle it follows that the accused has no obligation to say or to do anything. He just waits and sees what the Prosecution is doing, will they discharge itself of their burden or not? In that balance, you just sit there and listen and they have to prove. The disclosure obligation should be in a logical position in this balance, because you cannot require the Defence to provide the Prosecution with all kinds of information in order to allow them to discharge themselves of their burden of the proof. So, it is a principle here. It may not be in the Rules, but it follows from that principle that it is not a matter that should be decided specifically in the Rules. Again it is for you, as Judges, to decide the matter on your discretion following this principle, and that is what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, if Bassiouni says that our Rules come primarily, very strongly at least, they are based on US Federal Rules, in the US Federal Rules there is a requirement that the Defence provide its witness statements to the Prosecution after ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- after the witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it seems to me that -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That system functions in ----- 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the civil law system, of course, the investigating judge prepares -- you know more about this certainly than I do--prepares a dossier which, of course, would have witness statements for the Prosecution, witness statements for the Defence, and then gives it to the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right, but I have no obligation to disclose anything on my part.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand, but the investigating judge in the process may have statements of the Defence and these would go to the Prosecutor. All I am suggesting is that it is difficult to have it both ways, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sometimes -- the Prosecution does it too -- the Prosecution will say, "Well, you know, the Rules do not say this, or the Rules say that", and whatever. Of course, they say that, obviously, as advocates when it suits their purpose. I suppose I am just raising this with you to let you know the concerns that we have, because you are right, our Rules are derived from common law and civil law systems, but many writers have said that they are based primarily, as is the Statute, on an adversarial system. So then we, in applying these Rules, say to ourselves, "Well, do we look then to the adversarial system as these great writers have told us, perhaps, that we ought to do?" But now I hear you tell us that with respect to the quantum of proof required, which again is something that would fall under part 6, we should look to corroboration. Then, of course, your other 28 argument is that Rule 96(i) does provide for corroboration in sexual assaults.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand your position on that. One last question, it has to do with Article 7(1) of the Statute. That is an aiding and abetting provision. We received pretrial briefs from counsel some months ago, very lengthy pretrial briefs, where all of the crimes charged were discussed, or many of them at least, and elements were set forth and then the Defence took a position with respect to the elements that must be established, but no one mentioned -- the Prosecutor did not mention, you did not mention either -- Article 7(1). Now it seems to a great extent, perhaps, this motion may turn on our application of 7(1). I guess my question is that the parties wanted us to rule on the matters that you raised in your pretrial brief because you considered that you needed guidance in how to conduct this trial, and that you were pushing us very hard to make a ruling to the extent that there were differences in your position, which we found there were not that many differences, but in any case no one suggested that we should be looking at Article 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: From our point of view, that seems quite logical because you have to see the evidence first before you can judge what your position might be. That is the reason why I raise it now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am happy you have raised it now and that was the Judges' position as well, that what we do is we consider the 28 evidence as it comes in and then we will apply the law to the evidence that is adduced, but you were attempting to give us some guidance as to what elements formed a part of each of the laws that we were applying. Now you are saying that it is not enough for aiding and abetting to be a part, but that instead you have to be present. So what I want to ask you then is, if it can be shown that an accused was part of the transaction and if there is a transaction charged in a count, need it be shown that the accused physically participated in each of the acts charged in the count, or was even present when it was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have phrased it very carefully, and that is the reason why I have written it down.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, help me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Active involvement in the execution of the crime, and it is not enough to be present whilst the crime is committed if the accused takes no part in it and does not act in concert with those who commit it, unless he watched for his companions in order to permit the commission of the crime." That is the phrasing I used. That was very carefully drafted.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution must show that he watched for them for the purpose of showing that it was committed. The Prosecutor need not show that he was present, is that what you are saying then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is what I am saying. That is a very relevant position in this case, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You need not show that he desisted from this 28 participation. Like in a conspiracy -- are conspiracy matters considered in civil law systems? I know Mr. Kay is familiar with these.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, that point might be an issue to be discussed in count 1, but we are not dealing with count 1 in this motion, are we not?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have not included that in your motion for dismissal for dismissal of charges. But, in any case, your position then is that he must be present, but you must then show that he actively participated, when you say "actively", if there is a charge of beating, that he was one of the persons who actually did the beating or that he directed those persons at that time in the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, we even took a more simple position, acted in concert with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is more than directing; it could be any position that enables the others to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Like form the group and being the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Being a part of the group is not enough because members of the group may do things I was not aware of being a part of that group.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Whose burden is to show that an act that was done by a group that was formed was not in furtherance of the plan of the group?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would say the Prosecution will have to prove that there was any active involvement or a commitment of the accused 28 to what the group actually did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Actually participating, hitting is a beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is a very easy one. But I would say the Prosecution would have to prove that being in that group there was a commitment of the accused that he acted in concert, he did something that enabled the group to act as it did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: "Or giving approval", Judge Vohrah says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, for example. It should be any activity on the part of the accused on the basis of which the Prosecution can show from that activity it is proven that he participated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could it be construed -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Just standing there and doing nothing is not enough.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us focus on what Judge Vohrah just said, "giving approval": Could it be construed that the failure on the part of a member of the group to speak out and attempt to stop what was going on is constructive approval?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would say not because the passive acquiescence is contrary to our position that there is an active participation. You cannot simply suppose that someone had in his mind an idea and, therefore, you say, "Well, you had to do anything". No, it is not a matter of you had to do anything; the problem is you did something and, therefore, you are the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. A group of us are engaged in an activity, we will say beating, of a group of people. The beating involves four or five people, some of whom die. I actively participate and the group is composed, for the 28 purposes of our Statute and in this context as you have spoken about, of a group of Serbs, who are inflicting on a group of Muslims or Croats. It starts at X hour, and I engage in the beating of a couple of those people, perhaps even a killing of some of those people. It goes on, the transaction goes on, and one more is beaten, but I did not actually do the beating ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Of that last person?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- of that last person, yes, but I did do the beating of the others, some of the group of Muslims and perhaps Croats who were beaten, but I did not do the beating of the last one. I can only do so many. I did not actually do the inflicting on the last one, but I was there and I never disassociated myself from that beating; that would not be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If you phrase it that way, that would be enough.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Leave out "I did not disassociate myself", would it be enough if I was just there when that last beating, we will say, occurred or the next to the last?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would say whilst being in the group not actively been involved by doing anything and then disassociate myself from the group and later on -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Leave out "disassociation". I think you do not want to deal with that, that is too much, you say, is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Leave that out; you do not disassociate yourself affirmatively; you are just standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As long as you are in the group and you do not do 28 anything yourself, you are just there, that is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Considering that this is one -- that is another proposition you may not want to accept -- transaction, but a series of beatings that occurred on the same day, I actively participate in one or more of those, but then when we get to the last or next to last I am just there, I do not actually do the infliction, that is not enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would not say that. If a group is active at the place and you take an active part in what the group does, it is not relevant to me what happened, let us say, five minutes later, because you support by your own actions what the group does. What we are saying here is, if you are just there standing, looking, that is not enough. If you are just there standing, looking, and you do not prevent others in their actions, it is not enough. If you are just there, you are not actively involved and later on, separate from that group, you do things that had nothing to do with what the group did, you did not participate in the group.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But keep in mind now -- I want to make sure that you are following my example -- a group of people were beaten with the ethnicity set, I actively beat, I myself beat, one or more of those people, the beatings continue, I do not, however, actively beat one of those persons, but I am there when that beating occurs, is that enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is not enough.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are not actively involved because you do not 28 beat yourself or you do not encourage others to beat. You are not enabling them to beat.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So you then actually have to physically beat each of the persons, even though the beating was conducted by a group?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No. If you enable the others to beat, separate from beating yourself, you may enable others to beat by encouraging them, by advising them to do so, or commanding them to do so, because that is an activity that shows that you agree with what they do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you briefly about corroboration in the civil law -- assuming, perhaps incorrectly, that all systems of civil law are the same, but at least if you can tell me the system that you are familiar with -- take the case of a shooting which results in death witnessed by only one person: would I be right in thinking that there is no difficulty about conviction on the evidence of one person with corroboration being, I suppose, the discovery of the revolver, the tracing of the bullet as having come from that gun, and the dead body lying there? Would that be sufficient corroboration?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am afraid not because you need a link with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So that the fact that a thoroughly creditworthy witness says: "Yes, I saw that man discharge the revolver and the deceased fell down dead", that could not result in a conviction? 28

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I give you another example that may elaborate this problem? If someone is shot and the accused says: "I was there but I did not shoot him", his statement that he was there but he did not shoot him will do the trick, because that is an independent source which corroborates with the death of the victim. So, little may be enough, but it should be from an independent source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The independent source is not the identification of the gun in question as perhaps belonging to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are right, that is an independent source as such, but it does not link the event to the accused. The evidence should show that there is a link and that evidence should be corroborated. That is the position I have been taking here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That, you say, is the position in Dutch law, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There are, as usual, exceptions, for example, in rape cases and in other types of cases, but as a general rule ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The general rule I am thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- the unus testis nullus testis rule is firmly a rule in Dutch law. As a matter of fact, as far as I informed myself on this, it is a principle that is applied to other civil law jurisdictions too, though there are differences of course, but the bottom line always is you need corroboration. You could not simply link someone to an event if there is only one source. 28

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. Then we will hear from the Prosecution. (11.00 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who will present argument for the Prosecution? Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, in our submission, I will deal with the matters raised by Mr. Wladimiroff first and then I will just make a very few short comments about general matters following that. Your Honours, dealing firstly with the question of the fact that there is no provision in the Rules, which I believe was the first matter raised by Mr. Wladimiroff, it is our submission that this is a very significant aspect of the Rules that there is no provision contained in it for dealing with the no case to answer submission at the end of the Prosecution case. In our submission, the fact that there is very carefully laid out in the Rules the procedures to be followed at trial by a number of the Rules, and in particular but not limited to Rules 86, 87 and in particular 85, all carefully setting out the procedures to be followed, it is not just a matter of saying: "Oh, this is something that your Honours may rule under Rule 54". In my submission, Rule 54 should be interpreted in such a way that it gives the Court very wide discretion to make orders in relation to the preparation or 28 conduct of the trial. But, in so doing, our submission is your Honours should have regard to the other Rules that are contained in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and to be careful to ensure that this particular Rule, Rule 54, is not interpreted in such a way that other matters which are specifically and expressly provided for in the Rules are not ignored. In relation to that, your Honours, if one looks at Rule 86, one sees: "After the presentation of all the evidence, the Prosecutor may present an initial argument, to which the Defence may reply", namely, closing addresses and so forth. In our submission, this is a provision which expressly provides that the Prosecution may present such an argument, and if there was a no case submission raised at this stage and dealt with by the Court and the matter was dismissed -- let us assume there was only one count in the indictment -- then that Rule would not be satisfied it would be done so by general provisions such as Rule 54. When the issue of there being no rule relating to disclosure of Defence material was raised by your Honours, Mr. Wladimiroff responded that this was an issue that dealt with burden. In our submission -- I just quickly wish to dispose of this -- it does not only relate to burden at all. It is a question which goes to other matters which may assist the conduct of the trial. This was our original submission. For example, if the Defence made disclosure of a particular point, the Prosecution could stipulate to that point rather than need to call evidence. It also assists in conduct 28 such as an ability to immediately release the witnesses because the Prosecution does not know what is coming and at the end of evidence of the testimony of the witness there may be outstanding matters which could occur from other witnesses later in the trial, and the Prosecutor may say: "Well, we ask that these witnesses not be released because we cannot be sure what is coming up in the future". So these are the sorts of matters which arise when no statements are provided to the Prosecution and it does not go to questions of who has the burden of proof at all. It goes to the questions of the orderly conduct. Your Honours, Mr. Wladimiroff also seemed to place some -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not understand. So these are the sorts of matters which arise when no statements are provided to the Prosecution -- what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, when no statements are provided to the Prosecution, it must deal with the matter blind. It does not know what is coming forward. It may be that there are matters which the Prosecution may say: "Look, this is not in contest; if you wish to have a stipulation to this particular point, proceed and do so". But if we have no statements, we have no idea what the evidence is, we can never do that. So, I am saying these are matters which go to orderly and efficient conduct of proceedings as to be distinguished from the fact that we have the burden of proof from beginning to end, which is the point that Mr. Wladimiroff was making. It also 28 goes to the issue of whether or not witnesses can be released, because if we do not know what is coming, we say: "Well, we are reluctant to have this witness released because we do not know whether or not we may need to call back the witness at a later stage because of something that surprises us further down". I am only raising these as illustrations of why such disclosure goes to matters other than simply the burden of proof. Your Honours, Mr. Wladimiroff placed some emphasis on the basis that your Honours enquired as to whether there would be a no case submission. Very quickly I would suggest to your Honours that you should place no weight on that at all. Your Honours can ask a number of questions throughout the course of proceedings and in no way does that represent an indication of the existence of a provision or otherwise. Your Honours, dealing with the Rule 47 test which was raised by Mr. Wladimiroff, the test that is provided in Rule 47(1), it is our submission this is the only test that comes near to defining what is a prima facie case before this Tribunal. The word "prima facie case" appears in the Statute in Articles 18.4 and 19.1, 19 subsection 1, but there is no provision in there to tell us what it means. On a cursory glance of the provision, one may well conclude that it is a reference to a prima facie case as we know it at the common law. Also, in addition to that, prima facie case as we know it at common law at least in some common law jurisdictions is the same test that is applied at the committal hearing as is applied at the end of the trial. 28 So, in our submission, because the reference to Rule 47, the test to be applied there when the Prosecutor is satisfied that he can submit an indictment, is similar to the situation that existed at the end of a committal hearing or at the end of a preliminary hearing where the same test at common law applies, it is our argument that the same test should be applied at the end of the Prosecution case at trial, if any test is to be applied at all. I will come back to that because it is our submission that no such test should be applied at this stage of the proceedings. But, in any event, Rule 47 makes a specific reference to the necessity for evidence, and it is a sufficiency test. It reads: "In the course of the investigation the Prosecutor is satisfied that there is sufficient evidence". It is not as high a test as we have set out in detail in our submissions as the prima facie case, but it is a sufficiency evidence test. Mr. Wladimiroff also suggested to your Honours that the test that should be applied at this stage is the test that is set out in Rule 87(A) of the Rules. That simply cannot be right, in my submission. Rule 87(A), in the second sentence of that, provides: "A finding of guilt may be reached only when a majority of the Trial Chamber is satisfied that guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt". Surely, that cannot be the test because otherwise your Honours would be able to find the accused guilty of the crime now without the necessity of hearing from the Defence, which no one would be suggesting is the case, in our submission. There is no support for that anywhere that 28 we can find, at the common law or anywhere else, that the test to be applied at the end of the Prosecution case is the test of proof beyond reasonable doubt. It is a sufficiency of evidence argument. Indeed, in some jurisdictions there has been an issue relating to this about unsafe and unsatisfactory evidence. In those circumstances, it has in the past been held in some jurisdictions that if the resultant conviction would amount to a conviction which is based on unsafe and unsatisfactory evidence which would be overturned on appeal, then the Court at that stage could by its own motion dismiss the case. That has been held in a number of jurisdictions not to be the position, because it is a matter for the Appeal Court, and even though a Judge may see evidence which appears to be unsafe and unsatisfactory at this particular stage of the case, then it is our submission that the state of the law on that is that the matter should still go through to determination by the Jury. Mr. Wladimiroff made reference to the case of Van Beelen in South Australia. I do not have the decision with me and my recollection of it is somewhat poor, but I understand it to be a case dealing with similar fact evidence and that a failure to be able to prove each of the similar facts beyond reasonable doubt in proof of an event is a failure to prove the whole case. I think it has been overturned, if I remember. Dealing your Honours with Rule 7(1).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you move to 7(1), are you going to tell us more about the standard that should be applied or not? 28 I just have a few questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. The standard to be applied, i.e. the test that should be applied -- is that what your Honours are saying? The test to be applied if there is to be a ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The test, whatever word, the test or what standard should be applied. Rule 87 says, it is prefaced by saying: "When both parties have completed the presentation of the case", and then it goes on to provide that there will be deliberations and that there must be a finding of guilt that can be reached only when a majority of the Trial Chamber is satisfied that guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt. That is the only Rule that appears at least in part 6 with respect to the quantum of evidence or the standard or the test. So, the question becomes, (1) if we assume that this motion will lie at this time, where do we pick up the test? What you are saying is that the mention in Rule 87 of "beyond a reasonable doubt" is in the framework of both parties having completed their presentation of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Now we then go back to Rule 47, of course, which deals with the confirmation of a review of the indictment by a confirming Judge, should he decide to confirm. That is when we then say "reasonable grounds" in the Rule. The Statute however says "prima facie case". This is neither of those situations, where we are now. We are neither at the confirmation stage, because the indictment has already been confirmed by a Judge not in our Trial Chamber, but we are 28 neither at the presentation -- we are neither at a point when all evidence has been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say, of course, we do nothing, we do not even hear this motion, but assuming that we do, what standard do we apply? What test do we apply?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The argument I make on that, your Honour, is this, that the word "prima facie case" appears in the Statute. There is nothing in the Statute at all to instruct us as to what that means. One, looking at it, could say, presumably, it is applying to prima facie case as is understood at common law. However, in the application of that prima facie test, as it is reflected in the Rules, the reflection of it appears in Rule 47(A). So we there for the first time get some assistance in what the word "prima facie case" means, so far as the jurisdiction of this Tribunal is concerned. We see in Rule 47(A) "there is sufficient evidence to provide reasonable ground", etc. That is to be distinguished from prima facie case test at common law when one compares a number of jurisdictions. The test of common law is a higher test. It is our submission that because the equivalent situation at common law is that the test to be applied at the time of filing an indictment is the prima facie test, which is the similar circumstance as that set out in Rule 47(A), and that that same test, prima facie case, which is applied at the time of filing the indictment, is exactly the same test that is applied by the trial Judge when the Prosecution has finished its 28 case at trial, then our argument is that the Rule 47 test should apply in these proceedings at the time of the submission of the indictment and the time that the Prosecution closes its case, should your Honours determine that such an application is appropriate at this stage. We support that by saying that even though the Rule 47 test is, in fact, and can be argued to be, a lower test than the prima facie case test at common law, both tests are tests based on sufficiency of evidence, and because of sufficiency of evidence, then if your Honours are seeking or searching for an appropriate test to apply, it is our argument that, consistent with the common law practice, the definition that you have devised of a prime facie case should be applied in both instances, that is, at the time the Prosecutor submits his indictment where a sufficiency evidence test is devised and at the end of the Prosecution case. We say that your Honours are also safe in doing this because it is done by one of your brother Judges. It is one of your brother Judges who, presumably, has the training, expertise and skill to evaluate and assess the matter to ensure that when the matter proceeds to trial the accused is not going to be subjected to a prosecution where there is no merit. So, because it is a sufficiency evidence test, that is the standard that should be applied at the end and it also deals with the same issue, because the whole of the basis of this, in our submission, is that it is unfair to an accused to either indict him or to allow the matter to proceed after the 28 Prosecution case if the Court says: "Well, there is no evidence of this, you have made this allegation in the indictment that this accused has committed this crime, we have heard all your evidence, you tell us that is all the evidence, but there is no evidence; you cannot get a conviction based on this evidence", that is because there is no evidence. If your Honours find there is no evidence, then it is our submission that you can and should dismiss. Indeed, one could go further and say that the Prosecutor has an interest in ensuring there is a fair trial. One could say it is incumbent upon the Prosecutor to simply seek to withdraw it because there is no evidence and it is unfair for the case to go forward. So that the Court should simply intimate to the Prosecutor: "Mr. Prosecutor, what are you doing about this? There is no evidence to support this charge at all. Why are you proceeding with this case any further?" So it could be even be shifted back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are defining two, I think, considerations -- I think; maybe I am mishearing you. Judge Sidhwa (and you have cited this in your papers), in his review of an indictment under Rule 47, which requires reasonable grounds, said that "reasonable grounds, therefore, point to such facts and circumstances as would justify a reasonable or ordinary prudent man to believe that a suspect has committed a crime". OK. There is the standard that you would suggest, that is a standard that is imported from our Rule 47. The next question, though, becomes that in applying, 28 as is true with most situations, you set out the Rule and then you have to apply it, when you say "reasonable grounds therefore", your position would be reasonable grounds would be evidence, some evidence that would justify allowing the Defence to go forward, that is, denying the Defence's motion for dismissal of charges or their motion that says that there is no case, reasonable grounds. But, then in looking to determine whether there are reasonable grounds, you do not look to whether the defendant should be convicted but whether he can be lawfully convicted, that is, the question is not whether on the evidence as it stands at the end of the Prosecution case the accused ought to be convicted, but whether he can be lawfully convicted. In doing that, you say you do not look at the credibility of witnesses' inconsistencies; instead you look to see whether or not he could be lawfully convicted. My question then is there seems to be a split from listening to Mr. Wladimiroff's presentation when he says that he could only be lawfully convicted if there was evidence of corroboration, that is, testimony that the accused committed the act and then evidence of corroboration. Then he has explained to us what he means by corroboration. Can you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We submit that Mr. Wladimiroff is wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am not surprised if you say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We challenge him to produce any law in any jurisdiction which applies that test at this stage, as we submit there is no such law. There is certainly no such law at common law anyway. 28 There is no such law dealing with that being the prima facie test. Clearly, the prima facie case test is not whether the accused should be convicted at this stage or should be acquitted at this stage, but it is a question of, can he legally be convicted at a later stage? That is a separate test, because bear in mind, if your Honours please, that the whole basis of all of this comes from a situation where you have the Judge as the Tribunal of law and the Jury as the Tribunal of fact. The Judge never decides the issue on a question of fact ever at any stage. The Judge merely looks at the question of law, and makes a determination at that stage. The determination is, is there any evidence on which a jury could convict? They are not saying, based on the evidence a Jury should convict. That is not the question. It is, could they, and it is a legal question. That is why I mention the unsafe and unsatisfactory evidence, because there was a period of time in some jurisdictions where Judges sitting on a trial said to themselves: "If this matter goes on appeal, the Court of Appeal hearing this evidence is going to say: 'The evidence is unsafe and unsatisfactory'." A classic example is a situation where you have identification evidence, a fleeting glance. The Judge sitting on the trial says: "The jury may convict on it, there is evidence that says: 'Yes, I saw the accused run across the road, I did see it', so there is evidence there". But the trial

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SAYS
utterances.text: "But this would be unsafe to convict on this". Trial Judges, in those circumstances, historically in 28 the past for a period of time said: "We are going to direct the Jury, I will direct the Jury, to acquit because I know what will happen, that once this goes on appeal, this evidence is unsafe and unsatisfactory and the Appeal Court will overturn the verdict. Because we do not want to waste any more time, we do not want to put the accused to any more pain of having to go through the proceedings right up to an appeal to reach that stage, a fair trial dictates that the case should be dismissed at this stage on that basis". That has been overruled in numerous jurisdictions and is no longer the law. The position is that, notwithstanding that is the probable consequence of a Jury's conviction based on that evidence, the Tribunal of law must allow the issue to go to the Tribunal of fact so that it may determine the question. In my submission, that is why issues such as corroboration, issues such as the basis upon which a person is guilty of the charge, Rule 7(1), are not matters for consideration at this stage at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your submission you say that this whole notion of a motion for dismissal of charges, as the Defence has characterised it, or a motion for a directed verdict or a motion for judgment of acquittal, as you refer to it in your submission, is something that is peculiar to a jury system. But you know, and if Mr. Bassiouni is correct, that many of our Rules are based on US Federal law, you know that Federal judges may at the close of the Prosecution -- or Mr. Tieger knows, as you know about Australian law and, perhaps, American law -- case 28 in chief a judge in a non-jury criminal case may rule and grant a motion to dismiss if the judge finds that there is no evidence that the crime or crimes have been convicted. At that point may not the judge assess the totality of the evidence offered and say: "There is no evidence, there is something missing"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: An element that is missing, but that is a legal -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, if you reach that point that I am saying that is something -- it is not so much a prima facie case submission, which is again a different matter. In a situation where the Prosecution says that the accused did something -- indeed, imagine the following situation: The Prosecutor submits an indictment to the confirming Judge based upon a statement of a witness. That is the only evidence there is. It is submitted that way. The confirming Judge confirms the indictment. It comes to trial. At trial, the witness does not come up to proof or, indeed, the witness does not appear at all. At the end of the case, if that is all that there was ever in the case, one would expect the Court to say: "There is no evidence at all that supports this count. Is it not unfair that the accused should continue on with this matter for a minute longer in relation to that count where there is absolutely no evidence? In our submission, that is a different situation to the prima facie case test which we have set out in the Rules because it talks about a sufficiency of evidence test. There is a legal determination to be made. The legal determination to be 28 made is, could a legal conviction result as a consequence of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If a legal conviction could result on the basis of one witness's testimony, whose testimony addresses each of the elements ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- that are necessary, then that, you say, would be sufficient ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- without the need for corroboration?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you say about the fact that in Rule 96(i) there is a requirement of no corroboration in sexual assault cases, and Mr. Wladimiroff says that is an indication that there should be corroboration in all other cases. In many common law systems, I gather, but unlike the civil law system, as Mr. Wladimiroff seems to have told us, there is a requirement of corroboration in sexual assault cases. By putting that in the Rules -- it is not really important, Mr. Wladimiroff; in many common law systems there is a requirement of corroboration in sexual assault cases -- explicitly, what the Tribunal has said is that in this Tribunal no corroboration is required. Can you draw from that, though, the implication that in some draftings when you put something in specific, "no", it perhaps is interpreted that it is "yes" in other situations, if you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. No, in our submission, the answer to that is that 28 in the calendar of crimes that even our jurisdiction deals with, clearly, there is no support, certainly at common law, that requires corroboration. If corroboration is required for all of the crimes, it is our submission that that would have to be so specified. The fact that it is not so specified means that the issue is left open. I mean, in some jurisdictions there is legislation specifically saying: "Proof of this crime will require corroboration". It specifically and expressly deals with it. Sometimes that is developed as a process of the common law, but what is generally or what has been historically generally applicable is corroboration in rape cases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is required?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, in my submission, when your Honours drafted your provisions, your Rules, what we would be met with if there was no such provision as Rule 96(i) would be, obviously, when you look at the totality of the law in all the national jurisdictions, you must come down in favour of corroboration. Unless there was a specific provision saying that no corroboration is necessary, it is likely that your Honours would be so overwhelmed by the weight of all national law dealing with this that you would proceed to impose an obligation for corroboration in relation to rape. Clearly, it is our submission that when this was drafted it was intended to make it very clear that in rape cases, which are overwhelming cases where corroboration is 28 required, that your Honours want to make an exception. That certainly, in our submission, cannot then be extended to an argument to say, every crime, an assault, a beating, a deprivation of property, such offences which are in our Rules, also require corroboration, when in most common law jurisdictions certainly that I know of there is no such requirement. In our submission, that argument has no foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say there is no corroboration, one witness is enough, the standard should be whether there is no evidence to convict. Suppose we hear in this Tribunal from one witness who we just think is -- what is the word -- not being candid at all? One witness, we are not saying there is corroboration, but we just look at this witness and for a number of reasons -- you know, it is so difficult to assess looking at a witness -- for a number of other reasons, cross-examination, impeachment, that may result in impeachment, or in any case we make this determination -- can we make that determination, I guess, is my question. One witness, and we look at that witness, and based upon cross-examination which the Defence did not have an opportunity to do when the indictment was confirmed, and we say: "There is no evidence" because maybe from the testimony it is clear that the witness was not even there. He testifies, but it appears that he was somewhere else and that may be brought out on cross-examination. Can we not then say that the accused could not be lawfully convicted on that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In our submission, the situation there would be that if 28 the evidence is so contradictory, so unreliable and so incredible as to amount to no evidence, not a question of whether there is some evidence and it is unreliable or unpredictable or whatever, in a situation where you conclude that this is not evidence, it is so contradictory, so totally unreliable and unbelievable as to be the product of a disorderly mind, you might then say there is no evidence. But, in our submission, unless you get to that point, the matter should go on. It should go on, in our submission, in the absence of any provision for this procedure at all in the Rules and in the face of a specific rule which sets out the procedure at trial. There is, in our submission, a community expectation that once evidence is produced that the trial will go through to its conclusion and either side will make their submissions, the Tribunal of fact and law will retire and then return with its decision after all that process has been followed. If one were merely to interrupt the proceedings at this stage without the benefit of submissions from each side without hearing evidence from the Defence or hearing anything from the Defence as to what their position is, then, in our submission, there is an added element to this. The added element is that the community itself is not satisfied and that these proceedings would fail the community in that respect. It is not a question of the Prosecution expecting, hoping, relying on information coming from the Defence side which is going to assist it in its case. That is not the case 28 at all. The Prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt from beginning to end and it must do it on its own evidence, and it cannot expect any assistance from the Defence. But the community does have an expectation. When the community hears the evidence, then the community position on that is that that evidence should be dealt with by the whole process of the trial, and should be subjected to the benefit of submissions from either side. That is a community expectation which, in our submission, is an appropriate one for your Honours to have regard to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not understand what you mean by "community expectations".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, the scale of justice has two sides to it. When evidence is presented that something happened, there is an expectation that will be weighed. In the weighing process, the whole procedures of parties appearing before the Court and making submissions in relation to that evidence are factors to be taken into consideration when the determination of guilt or innocence is decided. To make a decision now, "We heard this witness and we do not believe that he is reliable and, therefore, we are going to dismiss the case" does not allow that process to run its course. In our submission, there is a disappointment by the community because that has not occurred. We submit that unless your Honours can say: "There is no evidence at all. In the absence of any evidence, you have no right being here", then, of course, if there is to be a fair 28 trial of the accused, the case should be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you something? Assuming for the moment, distasteful as it may be to you, that it is appropriate for this Chamber to apply a no case submission procedure, we are in the unusual situation that we do not have a jury. It is not a question of is this sufficient to go to the jury or not, because ultimately it comes back to us, as judges of fact. Add to that what may or may not prove to be the case, namely, that there may be no evidence at all called by the Defence other than alibi evidence, so that we are left with nothing more than the evidence that we have already heard from the Prosecution, and assuming that it is appropriate to have no case procedures, is there any different test to be applied at this stage from the test that we will ultimately apply in determining guilt and innocence after we have heard the evidence of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. If your Honours were to apply the prima facie test, that, in our submission -- this is the common law prima facie case test ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- forgetting Rule 47, if your Honours were to apply that test, that is a legal determination. It is not a question of deciding the facts. So it is a question of, can a person lawfully be convicted based on this evidence, and that is a sufficiency of evidence test. There is another test, if I may call it that, rarely ever seen happen, but a Jury of its own volition can take upon itself immediately following the 28 Prosecution case the decision and simply say: "There is no evidence here and on that count or on the whole charge we acquit". Without any intervention from the Judge whatsoever, the Jury is entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am not supposing for the moment that we are reaching that sort of extraordinary situation, but I am simply asking you, normally, if one is determining whether or not to leave something to the jury, one gives to the jury the right to determine the view they form as to the reliability of particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Therefore, the test that one applies at the no case stage is one more favourable, if anything, to the Prosecution than the jury may subsequently take. When we are both judges of law and also of fact, are there two different criteria that we apply, one at the no case stage and one at the ultimate conclusion stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. In my submission, there is no foundation that we can see in any jurisdiction for applying the ultimate test, proof beyond reasonable doubt, Rule 87, I think, that Mr. Wladimiroff spoke of. There is no law to support that anywhere that we can find which would be the test that you are applying at the end of the day when you are dealing with the evidence and deciding it as an issue of fact. As I come back to all the time, the only time you can do it, in our submission, is when there is no evidence and you can do it then. But, in our submission, Rule 87 clearly follows the 28 common law and clearly envisages that that test that your Honour spoke of, being unsettled about the evidence of a witness or whatever, is one that you deliberate on at the end of the case when you take into account the totality of all the evidence presented to you and the submissions of the parties. At that stage you make that decision. Yes, you are carrying the case forward to that period, to that point in time. Presumably, the Defence would argue: "Well, that is unfair". But, whether it would be unfair or not, the issue is there is nothing in any of the jurisdictions that we can point to or, we would submit, the Defence can point to to say that they are entitled to that determination being made at this stage in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
