utterances.text: So that in the United States system where there is a provision in non-jury criminal cases for a judge to conclude at the end of the Prosecutor's case in chief that the case should be dismissed, that in doing that the judge does not make a determination that the Prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, because in that instance the judge is the trier of fact and law. The judge does not make that -- you ask one of the American lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that is the law in the United States.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you do well with Australian, we have Dutch and British, so it is really very nice, not very limited -- but as the trier of fact and the trier of law, the judge would then be determining whether or not there is no evidence to justify a conviction in this case -- is that what you are saying -- but 28 not be determining whether or not the Prosecution has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In no evidence, what the Court would be looking at is whether or not, considering the elements of the offence, there is no evidence to prove that those have been met?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The decision of absolutely no evidence, of course, can be made right at the end of the Prosecution case. It can be done so without invitation. Your Honours can just decide it yourselves, in my submission. You do not need the Defence to make any submission to you. You do not need to decide yourselves in first instance, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before the Defence presents its case -- no?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the Prosecution case, if you decide there is no evidence on a particular point, you can do two things; you can dismiss the case there and then, or you can simply direct to the Prosecutor and say: "Why are you proceeding with this matter?"

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why can the Defence not file a motion to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Presumably, they could.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are saying they cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am saying they do not have to. I am saying they do not have to. Your Honours can do it of your own ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We can do it on our own motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Defence can interrupt the proceedings because of Rule 87. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not because of Rule 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission -- no -- it goes to, in fact, the right of a fair trial, that it is unfair in the absence of any evidence whatsoever to allow the proceedings to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it goes to the Articles themselves and the right of the accused to have a fair trial. Another matter I just wish to raise, if I may, your Honours, and that is it is hard for us to know or to predict that Benches in this Tribunal made up of common law Judges are going to deal with the matter differently to Benches made up of civil law Judges, but it is our understanding that -- it was our understanding -- there was no provision for a formal no case to answer submission to be made at civil law. We understand that cases may be dismissed where there is no evidence type situation, but we understood that there was no procedure for prima facie case. It seems to us, your Honours, that the bringing in of this procedure when there are no Rules whatsoever to specifically provide for it in the Rules may create complications for civil law Judges, for your brothers who are civil law Judges, who are not accustomed to such a practice. Unless there are any other matters, your Honours, that is our submission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you say about the position of the Defence that with respect to Article 7(1) of the Statute which 28 makes it a crime to aid, abet -- "a person who planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime referred to in Articles 2-5 of the present Statute shall be individually responsible for the crime". So, it is planning, preparation or execution. You did not address this in your pretrial brief, so even if we had told you what we thought about it -- well, we would not have because you did not ask us, but anyway that is a particular concern of mine. The Defence, if I understand its position, says that you have to show that, of course, the act was committed; you have to show that the person was there and the Prosecution have to show that the accused actively participated in that act, but by active participation you do not have to show that the accused actually inflicted the blow, if that is what it is, but that he somehow at that time acted to further the commission of the assault and the beating in that instance. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our position on that ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because your whole argument in your submission is that, well, you have charged persons with having committed these things, and it is true, in all of the counts you say -- I do not have it; I have the indictment but I have misplaced all my papers; no, I have very orderly put it in my book -- the first one that is the subject of the motion, you say: "During the period between June 1st through 31st July 1992, a group of Serbs, including Dusko Tadic, severely beat numerous prisoners, 28 including Emir Karabasic, Jasmin Hrnic, Envir Alic, Fikret Harambasic and Amir Beganovic, in the large garage building or hangar of Omarska camp. "The group forced two other prisoners, G and H, to commit oral sexual acts on Harambasic and forced G to sexually mutilate him. Karabasic, Hrnic, Alic and Harambasic died as a result of the assault. By his participation in these acts, Dusko Tadic committed", then count 5 you say grave breach, recognised Article 2(A), wilful killing, and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal". Then, of course, counts 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11, other allegations are made with respect to Articles 2 and 3 of the Statute as well as 7(1). So, you charge that a group of Serbs beat prisoners and a group of Serbs required individuals to sexually mutilate and commit oral sexual acts on a prisoner. So, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you consider is your burden at this stage when the Defence has filed a motion for dismissal of the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our position at this stage, your Honour, is that, firstly, it is not a matter that the Tribunal need consider at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Unless we decide to do it on our own?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but we submit that any possible theory of liability is sufficient for you at this stage; you do not have to concern yourself with finally determining the issue. It is a matter that, we would submit, is a matter for the final 28 addresses anyway, and perhaps in opening address it could be mentioned in different circumstances. But, notwithstanding that, a reading of Article 7(1) makes it very clear how broad. It is instructive, if I may, to just remind your Honours of the wording of it when it says that a person who planned -- a person who plans does not have to be present; you can be quite remote from the scene if you plan something -- again was instigated -- you may or may not be present and participate -- ordered -- you could be quite remote from the scene if you ordered it -- committed -- yes, one would suggest that you would probably have to be present but there may be even arguments about that -- otherwise aided and abetted -- one gets into a number of jurisdictional differentiations in relation to that; some jurisdictions say aiding and abetting requires you to be present, others say that you do not. It goes, "Aided and abetted in the planning", so you do not even have to directly have planned, "preparation or execution". So these words are so wide, in our submission, that it is only if you came to a conclusion that under no theory of liability was the accused guilty, and there is no evidence, the two factors, you might be minded to dismiss, but, in our submission, the wording is so broad in itself that that could not possibly be the case based on the evidence that you have heard in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you say when you have charged in the indictment that persons committed these acts, then it is your position that the accused need only be one of the persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Acting in concert or acting alone, either by a process 28 of direct involvement or in some other way, such as planning, instigating, ordering or otherwise. We say that your Honours do not have to decide that now, but come the final addresses, yes, your Honours would expect to hear very clearly from the Prosecution what its theory of liability is based on its indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we find that there is evidence to meet 7(1) of the Article, would not either at this stage, well, at the conclusion of the trial, at least, certainly by a preponderance of the evidence, the accused also be guilty of the substantive offences, or am I asking you to go too far since you had not addressed that for us initially?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We would say yes, that is open to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is similar to a conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Conspiracy, as an individual count, you would be guilty of conspiracy, but you would also be guilty, would you not -- or not, I do not know, you tell me -- of the underlying offences?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You could be both guilty of the conspiracy and the substantive offences. Both theories of liability could apply. Finally, perhaps I would have said, your Honours, under any test that can be applied the evidence is clearly sufficient, and there is no justification whatsoever, in our submission, for dismissal of any of the charges at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you about counts 18 through 20. You discussed it in your papers and, of course, the Defence pointed 28 it out in its motion for dismissal of charges. But, considering the standard that the Prosecution would want the Chamber to apply, is there any evidence that -- well, it is charged in the second paragraph, paragraph 9, the second sentence, "As the victims were removed in a wheelbarrow, Tadic discharged the contents of a fire extinguisher into the mouth of one of the victims. By his participation in these acts", it also refers to some acts that preceded this sentence, "Dusko Tadic committed", and then it is a grave breach, violation, crime against humanity as well as Article 7.1 of the Statute. Is there any evidence that the fire extinguisher was discharged? If so, point it to us in the transcript which we have read carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that, it is our submission that whether or not emptying the fire extinguisher or whether the person was alive or dead or whatever is one in a number of acts that are particularised in the indictment. The fact that there may not be evidence as to one particular that has been pleaded does not in anyway suggest that there is no evidence. There may be no evidence of that particular incident, but that does not of itself mean to say that the offence has not been proved because it is merely one of the particulars. So, if, for example, you had a charge of causing great suffering or whatever, the person was hit on the head, dragged behind a motor vehicle along a gravel road and then thrown into a pond, for example, it was pleaded, and at the end of the case the throwing into the pond aspect of the pleadings was not proved by the Prosecution, your Honours would not dismiss it. You would say 28 that particular has not been proved. It may be that if it was a particularly egregious act, your Honours would take it into account in sentencing and say: "Well, it has been alleged that this happened, it did not, and that seemed to us to be the most serious aspect of the offence", so, therefore, when it comes to sentencing you would take a different view than what you would if it was shown that the person was thrown into the pond. In our submission, that is how this should be dealt with at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is based on your assumption or your proposition, the correctness of the proposition, that you have asserted in your submission that this was all one transaction, and that Mr. Tadic was part of the first sentence, that is, causing persons to drink water like animals from puddles in the ground, jumping on their backs and beating them until they were unable to move -- you do not say "dead", unable to move -- but then when we get to the next sentence which deals with the fire extinguisher, as I recall the testimony, the witness was specifically asked: "Was the person in the wheelbarrow dead or alive?" The witness said: "No". But the witness was never asked whether the accused discharged the contents of the fire extinguisher into the mouth of one of the victims. Whether that victim be dead or alive, the point is there was no evidence that he discharged the contents. Is this a discrete charge, the second sentence, or is it part of the same transaction? Do we need to find that there 28 is evidence that Tadic either directly participated in the first sentence, or that it meets your version of the meaning of 7(1), and then disregard the second sentence that there is no evidence that the contents of the fire extinguisher was discharged? When I say "disregard the second sentence", having read the transcript, there is no evidence. There is not a word mentioned about it, so what do we do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In our submission, your Honours, what you do is you look at the whole charge, in our submission, and have regard to all of the matters particularised in the charge. Certainly, had there been evidence of the discharge of the contents of the fire extinguisher, we would be arguing that that is a matter to go to proof of the offence. But we do not only rely on that. If that was the only particular and it was the only thing we could rely on, yes, there would be no evidence. But that is not the case. We have the evidence of the accused being present. We have the evidence of the general event and the circumstances that happened. We say that the absence of just one component of the particulars does not in any way mean that there is no evidence in relation to the commission of the offence. It merely means that one particular has not been proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I take up that point? On a no case submission, assuming that that is going to happen, is there any advantage or is it at all proper when you have a charge such as the one that has just been discussed which contains two quite distinct elements, as it were, at least to narrow the issue that has to be dealt with by the Defence by indicating that the second of 28 those elements is one which need not be disposed of because there is no evidence relating to it?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just add to that approach, if it is charged that persons were beaten with steel bars, wires with balls, metal balls at the end, etc., and the last one is with wooden planks and there is no evidence that they were beaten with wooden planks, should we narrow the issue and say, you do not need to defend against wooden planks because not a word was mentioned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In our submission, your Honours, that is not necessary at this stage. Clearly the Defence know what the state of the evidence is. There is a transcript and they can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We would not be here if you two agreed on the state of the evidence. We would be hearing a witness I suppose -- but anyway, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But there is no notion that goes to the issue of whether or not the accused can or cannot have a fair trial based on whether there are particulars at this stage of the proceedings it looked like that they have not been either supported by evidence or proved. If I can move from the specific example to the more general example, you may have a situation where the Prosecutor has some theory of liability which would say that the accused is still implicated in this other particular which has been alleged in the indictment, notwithstanding that the accused was not present or participated in that event itself. So there may be other theories of liability which would be advanced. I am 28 talking in a hypothetical situation. For that reason, it is our submission appropriate to leave it to the end of the day. What should, in our submission, motivate your Honours is where you have a situation, what I was speaking of earlier, where there is just no evidence of this ever happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I take up your excellent example about the motor car and the dragging along the road and then the throwing into the pond? There is a no case submission, and in fact it turns out from examination that there is no evidence at all about throwing into the pond. Is it (A) useful, (B) proper for the Court to say: "Well, as far as throwing into the pond is concerned, there is no evidence and the Defence need not trouble with that. As to the other two elements, yes, there is a case to answer"? Is that improper or is it useful?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It would not result necessarily in the dismissal of a count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we what we are talking about is narrowing the evidence. This is just one incident, but in terms of the efficiency of the trial why should the Defence be put to the task of trying -- they would not even be put to the task -- to dissuade of something when there has been no evidence. They might even, if they choose, be prejudiced if they were forced to deal with that inadvertently, but it would not happen because of very competent counsel, offering evidence that might help the Prosecution to overcome this lack of evidence. But that would not happen. Mr. Kay says, God forbid! So why do that? Why not 28 just say: As to that incident we will exclude it, and that is assuming that we would keep in counts 18 through 20 as it relates to the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we go back to the circumstances where a no case to answer submission is generally made at the end of the case for the Prosecution, this is not a matter that arises at that stage. What happens is that the judge considers the issue of law and says: Is there any evidence to go to support this count? If the judge says, yes, there is, the jury are never informed of the fact that a no case submission has been made. So the indictment is not amended at that stage. But when the judge is summing up to the jury he might well say, and properly should say: "Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, the prosecutor in his indictment you have before you has alleged that this event happened. We have both sat here and listened attentively to the evidence and we have not heard any evidence of that. So clearly, you cannot rely on any inferences, draw any inferences" or whatever he might say, "from the fact that it may have happened, it could have happened, it should have happened or whatever, you have heard no evidence of it." Then he would deal with it at that point, but that is dealt with at the conclusion of the case after the submissions have been made. In my submission, if your Honours are to truly apply the no case to answer submission as it is understood, then, no, it is not appropriate at this stage to require an amendment to the indictment. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Wladimiroff, rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will try not to repeat myself and confine it to some issues, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As you wish, Mr. Wladimiroff. You may respond to any of the points that the Prosecutor raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It seems to me, your Honours, that the whole debate comes down to the question: What would happen if we would have rested our case? Then the evidence submitted by the Prosecution should be sufficient, according to the standard of Rule 87, would it not? We have not informed you that we will rest our case. We have informed you that we will present our case and we have informed the Prosecution that we will present our case in the context of alibi witnesses. So, as a matter of fact, by not resting our case but by presenting our case in the context of alibi witnesses, still the standard is: Did the Prosecution by submitting the evidence meet the standards of 87? Discussing the standard here, it seems that the Prosecution has a lot of trouble with accepting that the standard of Rule 87 should be applied here, and they argue that 47 is the correct standard here. As we see it, what would be the sense of repeating the standard of Rule 47 at this stage of the trial? We feel it would not add anything to what has already been applied at the stage of presenting material to the confirming Judge. It seems logical to me that after the material has been presented to confirming Judge, and if that material was sufficient, then in trial it may appear that the witnesses do 28 not say the same things as they said in the interviews. That is what the confirming Judge had seen. He saw material which has not been said under oath in court or examined by either party. So in court you may have quite different situations there. The witnesses might not repeat what they have said in the interviews shown to the confirming Judge. So the test could not be the same in court. It would not make any sense to repeat that test of 47. What then should be the test in court? Here we have some confusion about the term "prima facie case" because the Prosecution simply wishes to use that term in the sense as it has been used in the Statute. But that term as it has been used in the Statute is confined to the pretrial stage. It has nothing to do with the standard that should be applied in trial at the stage where we are now. Then he is arguing about the term "prima facie case" and that common law has a different understanding if you deal with that in a trial. Then he explained how it works with a jury. Indeed, the judge will instruct the jury on the basis of the law. In that context the term "prima facie case" appears again. But here we do not have a jury, so the term "prima facie case" cannot simply be transported into the proceedings of this Tribunal. It may have its own meaning in the context of your Rules, because you are not only the Tribunal of the law, you are also the Tribunal of the fact. There is no jury to instruct. You instruct yourselves. So we feel that here the standard would be the 28 standard that a judge dealing with the law and dealing with the facts should apply. The only standard you can apply dealing with those aspects is the test of 87. Again, that makes sense because you would have to apply that standard when we had rested our case. So once again, we feel that the only proper standard here is the standard of 87: Did the Prosecution fulfil their obligation to prove their case? Going into that test, there is a lot of discussion possible on the issue, did they or did they not, and we have set out in our motion why on certain aspects they did not. We suggested to your court by applying that standard that you should also take into account specific aspects of civil law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you move on to that, let me ask you two questions dealing with the first two points you made. You have indicated that you would just be presenting alibi testimony. In fact, at least from your witness list now, we are going to be hearing, maybe today, from a policy witness and we will be hearing -- I do not have the list before me -- from several witnesses. I do not know what they will testify to, but they are going to talk about the events. So I do not know that even based on the witnesses you have listed, they are only dealing with alibi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But the other thing, though, is that the witness list, as for the Prosecutor, has been supplemented. They had actually a "will call" list and then a "may call" 28 list. So it may appear as this fluid trial proceeds that you may wish to add additional witnesses, and that is something we would have to consider. I do not know at this point whether that is going to be the case, one, based upon the witnesses whom you have already listed and then there again may be some change. Even if it is alibi witnesses, I do not know what exactly the extent of that will be and I do not even want you to tell me. Will it be that the accused was not there or some other kind of alibi, like there was a witness who saw what happened and that is not what happened? I do not know at this point whether the evidence that you are going to offer will not get into the occurrences, the actual occurrences, as opposed to the witnesses simply not being there. I understand what you say, but it is fluid. Can you address that first question? Then I have one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will. What I am saying here is in the context of those charges in the counts as addressed in our motion. So I am not dealing with count 1. When I say that we will represent present only alibi witnesses on that issue, you will recognise that in the motion we did not touch the specific elements that make an ordinary crime a war crime or a crime against humanity.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Also you did not address 29 through 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. So when I am saying "alibi witnesses" I am not referring to expert witnesses because they deal with those expert specifications which are not in our motion. The motion only deals with behaviour: Was he participating or was he not? 28 If he was participating, we did not touch on the issue of what does it mean in terms of: is that an ordinary crime or a crime under your jurisdiction? So when I say "only alibi witnesses", I am referring to those witnesses who deal with the charges in the motion, who will deal with the allegation that he participated. Indeed you are right when you say we may have two classes of witnesses: those who were there and say, "I have seen what" happened, but no Dusko Tadic was there", or if I am cynical, "He did not beat them with the left hand as the witnesses said, but he did with his right hand." We are not going to present this class of witnesses. We will present witnesses who will testify about where was he at that time, not there at least.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except as to count 1 and counts 29 to 34?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We did not touch on that because some discussion might be possible and we would like to continue that discussion while presenting our case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not having heard the witnesses testify, I do not know that we can say with certainty what they will testify to. Good lawyers always talk with their witnesses and discuss their potential testimony, but as we have seen thus far some witnesses go way off field and, particularly with the language problems we have had, many other things are gotten into. I do not know that we can be so certain about what is going to transpire during your case as opposed to what you would hope would transpire. That is a concern that I have. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that, your Honour, but as you already said, and you were certainly not joking, the Defence will not submit additional evidence to the allegations of the Prosecution by presenting witnesses in court. So what is the relevancy of our witnesses testifying perhaps on other things than alibi?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exactly. Well, I do not know. My real position is that I do not know. I just know that I wish the trials were held the way that was written in black and white with all of the periods and everything, but unfortunately it does not happen and we as Judges and lawyers have to accept it. But I understand what you have said. The other thing, though, I guess relates to what witnesses have said that was different in their prior statements than what they say under oath. You say that the test should not be the same. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It cannot be the same, because what the confirming Judge saw was material based on the interviews, excerpts, sometimes the interview itself perhaps, what the witness told the interviewer. Judging that, it is just a reasonable grounds test, nothing more than that. But when the witness appears in court giving his evidence under oath being examined and cross-examined, the quality of that information is quite different. Then the test is a different one for that reason. You cannot simply say: Is there reasonable ground for listening to the witness? The test then will be: Is there good reason to believe that the evidence he is giving is right and truthful?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As he also looks at the Judges too I hope that that changes his approach, and having prepared in advance with 28 the Prosecutor or the Defence his testimony might be very different and of a different quality when he comes to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what we should be looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I would say then indeed it is evidence before the confirming Judge. Although the Rules use the word "evidence" it is not evidence. It is material given to the confirming Judge and the status of that material is different to what you have heard in court. That is evidence. I have a little problem with the approach of the Prosecution that the Court should address community expectations. I would say that, on the contrary, the Court is a filter against community expectations. The Court is not here to please the community. The Court is here to decide whether Dusko Tadic is guilty or not, and that is the test we ask you to apply. So I am not really impressed by the argument. I think it is highly invalid. You should certainly not decide the matter on the basis of what will the public say if we dismiss or limit the charges to a certain extent, because that is not the point. The point is: is there a case to answer? That is exactly the standard you will apply on the basis of Article 87.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought what Mr. Niemann may have been referring to was the right of the Prosecutor to receive a fair trial, and the Prosecutor representing -- I suppose in this Tribunal we had much discussion about what we would even call an indictment, but we decided the Prosecutor versus the accused. So the Prosecutor represents someone. I thought he was 28 referring to Prosecutor's right to have a fair trial, but I can assure you we are not concerned with community expectations, as you have described them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You raise an interesting point. Does the Prosecution have the right to a fair trial? I am not going into that matter. Let me just see from my notes if there is anything left which I should address. No, otherwise I will repeat myself. I think I have said what I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber decides to accept this motion and rule on it, is that appealable, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: From my memory I say that part (B) of 44 -- no, it is not 44. It is 72. A very tempting question, your Honour, because you changed the Rules in the meantime, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, 73 deals with preliminary motions but there is a new Rule with respect to appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about these changes later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is a new Rule with respect to appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It might be an idea to have these changes sent to the Defence and the Prosecution right away so we are aware of what is at stake here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I must admit I do not have a copy of it here either, but I will get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So I cannot answer because it may depend on those amendments you have made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What the Rule -- well, you have it -- Rule 72 sub-rule (A) remains unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But (B) may have been changed. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Then (B) reads now: "The Trial Chamber shall dispose of preliminary motions in limine litis and without interlocutory appeal, save, (i) in the case of dismissal of an objection based on lack of jurisdiction, where an appeal would lie as of right; (ii) in other cases where leave is granted by a bench of three Judges of the Appeals Chamber, upon serious cause being shown, within seven days following the impugned decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not quite sure what means "a serious cause", you see. It is a new Rule and we did not quite study that. As I said, we just stumbled over it. We were not aware that you changed it. So I am not able to address that problem now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is leave by a bench of three Judges of the Appeals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We might test that. As a matter of fact, it is an issue we do not need to address now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As a Judge I am always kind of looking ahead and trying to plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No Judge wants a notice of appeal on his or her decision.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It will not make any difference in terms of our decision, that is for sure, but just in terms of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: To be frank with you, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That makes sense. Is there anything else, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, what do you think about the recent 28 amendment to Rule 72(B): "In other cases where leave is granted by a bench of three Judges of the Appeals Chamber, upon serious cause being shown, within seven days following the impugned decision"? If you do not know either, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I really think, your Honour, it boils down to perhaps what is a preliminary motion, but because it is the final disposal of the matter it may be -- if it was against the Prosecution it was decided that the charge was dismissed, it may amount to final disposal of the matter. But I would really like to take this matter and consider it before answering your Honour in detail on that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If a charge were dismissed I presume then -- I can say this with certainty -- that the Defence would not offer evidence on that. Then if it were carried with an appeal, should there be an appeal after the trial, the only issue then before the Trial Chamber -- I am thinking out loud -- the only issue before the Appeals Chamber would be whether or not the Trial Chamber erred in granting the motion to dismiss charges, applying the standard that we would apply and then we would see whether the Appeals Chamber would accept the same standard. But in the absence then of any evidence by the Defence, would there be a new trial or what about double jeopardy? In our Tribunal Rules, unlike the common law system, the Appeals Chamber may take new evidence, which is absolutely foreign I suppose to our common law system and I do not know whether that problem might be cured that way to avoid any double jeopardy, that is something we really have not talked about. 28 I wanted your opinion. It is not really necessary. We will Rule and then you lawyers can decide and the Appeals Chamber, if it is applicable, can decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might just say, if it is of any assistance, your Honour, that the wording of Article 25 has always been a bit curious in terms of what the Prosecutor's rights of appeal are. Just dealing with Article 25, it specifically deals with persons convicted in relation to the Defence, but the Prosecutor's position may be different because it goes on and says, "From the Prosecutor on an error of law invalidating the decision" and so forth. Possibly there is a difference there, but I think I would assist your Honours better if I had some time to consider it and come back with a more reasoned decision on that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may draw your attention to Rule 115. It seems to me the only additional evidence might be submitted that was not available to it at the trial. So following your thoughts about the risk, what happens if you rule on the matter in appeal, I would say it is a limited issue then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The question then is what is the meaning of "not available", because our other Rule on review -- well, 115 deals with additional evidence and that is dealing with the appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we have another Rule.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have another Rule which deals with request 28 for review which then says that where a new fact has been discovered which was not known to the moving party at the time of the proceeding before a Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber, etc., etc., then you make a motion and you would then go before the Chamber and present evidence. So the question is, since 119 says, "A new fact has been discovered which was not known to the moving party", then should you look at 115 and assume that the words "not available" mean "not known", because "not known" is dealt with in 115. So "not available" could possibly be interpreted as ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The only suggestion I want to make is that it is a limited problem. Does it mean that the whole trial in all its extensive aspects will have to be repeated?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else with respect to the motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will accept your submissions and take this matter under advisement and rule as quickly as possible, perhaps by tomorrow, certainly the next day. I understand this week you have only been able to present this one witness. I received your letter that went to Miss Featherstone. In the future, please, if you would send your communications to the Registrar with a copy to the Prosecution rather than Miss Featherstone. But it was brought to our attention and we understand that you have a problem with your witnesses just in terms of their availability because your other expert witnesses have to be somewhere else as expert 28 witnesses are. But, as we told the Prosecutor very forcefully, please do not require that we have any dead time. We are very anxious to move as efficiently as possible, so tell your expert witnesses that I know they have other things to do but we are anxious ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Normally, it would not be a problem because we would have filled the gap with our witnesses of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand about the election and you could not bring them forward, but I am referring to the expert witnesses. But, having been in that situation, I know sometimes you have difficulties with them, but impress upon them our desire to move forward. But, as I indicated, we will rule on your motion for dismissal of charges as quickly as we can, perhaps tomorrow, certainly by the following day. The only witness you have this week is an expert witness, so I do not think that his testimony will be impacted by the motion pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good. Then we will rule as quickly then as we can. You will then be ready, Mr. Wladimiroff, to proceed with that witness at 2.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Fine. No problem whatsoever. I have some logistical issue, though, relating to the video link. I am not sure whether we can deal with that in open court or closed court. It may have to do with how we are going to execute that. I prefer to deal with it in closed session so we can 28 talk freely about it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That might be good and it might be helpful if we even have the Registrar present because I know there have been comments ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So if we start this afternoon, perhaps, with that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would like to do that? That is OK. We will stand in recess until 2.30. At 2.30 we will be in closed session and we will then discuss those issues. How long will that take? Maybe 15, 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who will be handling the testimony of your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will be, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence calls Robert McBeth Hayden. MR. ROBERT McBETH HAYDEN, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that has been handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Orie, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Would you please state your full name sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Robert McBeth Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, were you born on 19th January 1950?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Hertford, Connecticut, United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court what position you hold presently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am now an Associate Professor of Anthropology at the University of Pittsburg.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any degrees from universities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hold a law degree from the State University of New York at 28 Buffalo and a PhD in Anthropology also from the State University of New York at Buffalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, what position did you have before joining the University of Pittsburg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Project Director at the American Bar foundation in Chicago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, Professor Hayden, what your professional work focuses primarily on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My professional work focuses primarily on laws, constitutions, politics and culture in the former Yugoslavia and its successor republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Since when have you done research on these subjects, Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I began doing research on these subjects in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever live in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lived for more than four years in the area of the former Yugoslavia beginning in 1981 when I held a Fulbright Fellowship for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did you live on later moments in that or just in 1981 to 1983?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have gone very frequently to the former Yugoslavia since 1981. As I say, I have spent more than four years in the country since then, in the area since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, do you speak the language or the languages of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak what I learned as Serbo-Croatian which is now called Serbian Croatian and Bosnian otherwise, but I still speak Serbian Croatian. I am not a native speaker by any means but 28 I am quite fluent in the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you tell us something about your publications on the issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been publishing on these topics in the former Yugoslavia since the mid 1980s. My earliest work was on the self-management court system, and I actually published a book on the Yugoslav self-management court system. I am probably the only expert in the world on that topic. However, as events began to develop in the former Yugoslavia in the late 1980s, things began as constitutional crises, and I switched the focus of my work to the constitutional crises and the political and cultural issues that drove them. I published a number of articles in professional journals since then on these topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What is your present research focusing on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment, I am engaged on a project on, essentially, the retreat from democracy in Serbia and Croatia since 1980, since the democratic elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, Professor Hayden, how your research was financed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My work has been financed by grants that I have obtained in competitions, nationwide competitions, in the United States through such funding agencies as the National Council Facility of East European Research, the International Research and Exchanges Board, the American Council of Learned Societies and Social Science Research Council and the Fulbright Commission. I have also held a Fellowship from the Guggenheim Foundation. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: How do you follow at this moment the events and how did you follow during the last couple of years the events going on in the former Yugoslavia, Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I followed the events in part by going to the former Yugoslavia. Since 1990, since December 1990, I have gone there -- I was there for four months in 1990/91, was not there in 92, went briefly in 93, went for several months in 1994, made two separate trips in 1995 and I have just returned from two months there. I also followed events in the former Yugoslavia through the Yugoslav media which I receive in Pittsburg and also, of course, through the Internet which is an extraordinary resource of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, have you ever been consulted by any government or by any government official?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been consulted by agencies of the United States government. I was also a consultant to Mr. Milan Panic at the time of the London conference on Yugoslavia in August '92 for a total of five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did this give you extra access to information and documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly, yes, did get access to information at that time that I would not have had as an academic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, have you read the transcript of the Tribunal that contains the testimony given by Dr. Gow in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain, in addition to what you have said already, what the sources are of your knowledge and of your expertise? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, of course, in the course of my research gathered a great deal of material, some of it from published sources, from the media, some of it government documents and other unpublished materials. Of course, I have gathered a great deal of information through my discussions, through formal interviews and informal discussions with people in the various parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You have also consulted legal texts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have also consulted legal texts and, of course, I do quite a lot of reading of the works of my academic colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you please give us an explanation of what the word "narod" means in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Narod"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: "Narod".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Narod" is usually translated as "nation" and occasionally as "people". It is related, closely related, to the verb "rodati" which means "to give birth".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 19 to the witness. (Handed) Professor Hayden, Exhibit 19 has been introduced by the Prosecution as the text of the federal constitution of 1974. I assume that you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is the constitution -- the English translation of the constitution of 1974, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please explain to us how the sovereignty is structured, to whom belongs the sovereignty under the federal constitution of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. I think that in looking at sovereignty decision, it is 28 important to consider what the state is there to do, to whom does the state belong? For example, the United States is considered to be a state of equal citizens, and this is implied in the preamble, "We, the people". When we look at the Yugoslav federal constitution of 1974, we find a form of dual sovereignty in which the state is there to serve, to advance the interest, to represent the interests of, on the one hand, the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia and, on the other hand, the working class and all working people, remembering that this is very much of a socialist constitution. It is designed to set up a socialist state and a socialist state is there to serve the -- to advance the interests of the working class and all working people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you refer to the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia, could you please explain to us how this relates to the expression you just explained to us of the word "narod"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Narod" has the connotations that are in the English word "ethnic group". This is why I say it is related to the verb "to give birth". So that the phrase "nations and nationality", "narodi, narodnosti", is universally taken, simply understood to mean, on the one hand, the "narodi", the "narods", the state forming nations, the Croats, Serbs, Slovenes, Muslims Montenegrins and -- who did I miss -- and, on the other hand, the "narodnosti" which would be minority groups in English parlance, such as Albanians, Hungarians, peoples who had a state of their ethnic group outside of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about state forming nations, do I understand 28 well if these are basically ethnical groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would certainly define them that way in English. One is a Serb through birth or a Croat through birth or a Slovene through birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, does or perhaps I should say did the 1974 constitution contain any provisions on the equality before the law of all citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does, but I -- would it be useful if I were to take a look at some of the clauses in the federal constitution that indicate the .....

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I will first ask your Honours: Professor Hayden has some of the Exhibits already in front of him and made some notes in order to find easier his way through. I do not think that would be a problem, but if it would, I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Those are exhibits that have been offered by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Mainly exhibits offered by the Prosecution, but in order to find his way through rather complicated exhibits that will be presented later on, he will have copies of these exhibits as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is no problem with him referring to notes. I suppose if he is going to refer to an exhibit, though, that is not in evidence, he should tell us that and then it should be marked and admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, it is just finding his way through numbers, etc., perhaps dates. (To the witness): Could you tell us in what provisions you find these equality provisions? 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The equality provisions of the federal constitution, I believe article, as I recall, I think it is 154, "Citizens shall be equal in their rights and duties regarding their nationality, race, sex, language, religion, education and social status. All shall be equal before the law", and I believe 249, if I can find it .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Hayden, we have the same problem going through mounds of exhibits we have, so take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 244, 245, I am getting close, 249. Right, "Yugoslav citizens shall" ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if you read these parts I hear that some people here at least have some problems in following you because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, I am sorry. It is also particularly a problem for the translators, I know. "Yugoslav citizens shall have a single citizenship, that of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Every citizen of the Republic shall simultaneously be a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia", but I think most importantly in this context, "Citizens of a Republic shall on the territory of another Republic have the same rights and duties as the citizens of that Republic", of the said Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, were any substantial amendments adopted to this 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a number of important amendments were made to the 1974 constitution. In 1988, what happened was that throughout the 1980s the Yugoslav Federation was going through a period of 28 protracted economic crisis that brought about a crisis of the peculiar, certainly unique, system of socialist self-management that had been created in Yugoslavia and embodied in the 1974 constitution. I would prefer not to give a lecture on Yugoslav self-management today, but I would simply say that the 1974 constitution contained a great deal that was devised of many provisions, many articles were there to structure the socialist self-management economy. In 1988, amendments were passed and there were two sets of issues. One of such issues had to do with the nature of socialist self-management. The other set of issues had to do with the nature of the relations within the Yugoslav Federation. There had been a certain amount of academic writing and some political discussion about the inefficacy of the Yugoslav Federation which did not, for example, have anything comparable to the commerce clause of the US constitution. So that, on the one hand, there was seen to be a need to revise the constitution, to remove the structure of Socialist self-management -- and, of course, many laws would be amended in this way too -- and, on the other hand, there was a need felt by some analysts and politicians to strengthen the structure of the Federation as a Federation. It was a very weak Federation in constitutional terms. In 1988, a quite massive set of amendments was passed to the federal constitution. I think there were approximately 30 amendments, and they mainly had to with -- in fact, they 28 almost exclusively had to do with removing the socialist self-management system that was seen to be a failure in economic terms. Proposed amendments to the strengthen the federation did not at that time pass. One of the effects of the amendments was to drop many references, all of the references, I think, in fact, to the working class and the working people that had been strewn throughout the 1974 constitution. If I may show you a bit of what I mean? I have brought a marked up copy of the constitution, but I would like to refer -- this is Exhibit 19 -- to show what you mean about the ways that sovereignty, the point that the state was divided ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Professor Hayden, if you are referring to one of the Exhibits, and we are talking about ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- Exhibit 19, perhaps it could be put on the screen and if you point at any particular part out of it that we see it on the screen so that it is better ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would anyone like to help me with this?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think so. Professor Hayden, with respect to the socialist self-management, are you referring to the management by the individual republics that was occurring under the 1974 constitution and then in 1988, to strengthen the federation so as to have more control over the republics, and give the republics less autonomy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, not exactly. The socialist self-management system -- you know, we could go into this very deeply but I am 28 not sure that you would want to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You said you did not want to -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The socialist self-management system was Yugoslavia's unique contribution to socialist theory. This was what set Yugoslavia off conceptually from the East European communist countries, and immediately after Stalin in 1948 the idea was to take seriously the view that workers should manage their own affairs under self-management. It was a very curious system. Business organisations were broken up into basic organisations of associated labour, which might be one workshop in a factory might be a basic organisation of associated labour and another workshop would be another basic association of associated labour. They would form a combined organisation of associated labour, and within these basic organisations the workers would meet, would have workers' meetings, that was a Workers' Council, and they would discuss matters. It was a quite extraordinary system that I do not think has been matched anywhere else, and the conclusion was reached in the 1980s that it did not work. Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think that is enough. I was focusing on something else. I may be wrong then about the effect of the 74 constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for these purposes ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I think you were at a point of indicating to us, perhaps giving just a few examples, of how these amendments would change the constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have marked quite a few, and maybe I do not have to, 28 this is actually a photocopy of Exhibit 19 that I have made. The reason I did so was that I marked certain passages so that they would be easy to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you could give just a few examples instead of having another Exhibit. The text is the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same, and if you would look on page 6 of Exhibit 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could page 6 be shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Put page 6 on. If we look here you will see: "The working people and the nations and nationalities shall exercise their sovereign rights". Now, this is a type of formulation that we find strewn throughout the document, "the working people and the nations and nationalities". Similarly, in the next paragraph: "The working people, nations and nationalities". These are examples of what I meant by the dual sovereignty. If we turn to page 15 of this -- and I really will not go through all the ones that I marked -- here: "In the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia all power shall be vested in the working class in alliance with all working people in towns and villages". This is a very ideological constitution. Similarly, page 21, right under VI, the Roman VI: "The working people and citizens, nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia are determined to", so this is an expression of who was the principal political -- who are the principal political actors in this state. Similar constructions are found throughout this constitution. I can point them out, if you wish. What happened 28 with the amendments, among other things, the amendments in 1988 was that these references to the working class and all working people were dropped from the constitution to remove the socialist ideological structure from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from these references to the working class, you mentioned two aspects, the other one was some political attitude changing, change in political positions. could you relate this in any way to the -- let me first ask were these changes in the minds of politicians of a nationalistic character or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the 1980s, what began as an economic crisis, in the early 1980s, came to be a political crisis. There was increasingly the perception that the economy was failing, not only because the socialist self-management system was cumbersome and inefficient, but of course European socialism was undergoing profound crises at the time. Yugoslavia, while not officially a one party state, effectively was one under the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and there was increasing discussion throughout Yugoslavia in the 1980s of the need to reform the political system. What began in the early 1980s as demands for the reform of the political system -- I could cite books by well-known scholars and others who argued for this -- came as the 1980s progressed to be increasingly demands for moving away from the one party system under the control of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. I should say, by the way, that in the 1974 constitution the leading role of the League of Communists of 28 Yugoslavia had been pointed out. This was also removed in 1988. What would follow communism? What would follow state socialism? There was a tendency in the western world to look, to take seriously primarily those who said that they wanted to replace communism with a civil society and western style democracy. However, throughout this period increasingly opponents of socialism were putting forth nationalist ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could I please ask you, talking about nationalist, could you please explain what you understand exactly under these circumstances under nationalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic principle of nationalism, as I am using it here, is the idea that each nation, ethnically defined, should have a state. You might view the nation as the group, the state as the territory and the government. This is a classic central European formulation since for the last 200 years this nation state idea does not work very well in English, in part because we have a different emphasis on the word "nation". For example, in American terms, if we say the president addresses the nation, he is addressing all the citizens of the country. But if we say, the President of Croatia, for example, is addressing the nation, he is addressing Croats and he makes this very clear in his form of address. The idea of nationalism is that the nation, the Croats or the Slovenes or the Serbs or the Macedonians or the Montenegrins should have the state, that they should be sovereign in their own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was this development only on the federative level or would you 28 find the same in the republics as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not really on the federative level, and this was why you did not get amendments to the federal constitution in 1988 that would have given any authority to the federal government to regulate, for example, economic transfers. Part of the nationalist idea was that this group, this nation -- and when I am using "nation" here, it has the ethnic connotation -- that this ethnic group would be sovereign in its own state, and sovereignty was interpreted as meaning that it could not be subordinated to any other structure specifically and including specifically the federal structure of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to present a document to you together with an English translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How is that marked, Mr. Orie? Is that going to be an exhibit of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to tender that document after Professor Hayden has explained what it is, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. This is -- it is called "The Hero". It is in Slovenian and it is a photocopy of the Journal of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia and the Assembly of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for parliamentary groups and delegations. In other words, it is a Slovenian parliamentary document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document as exhibit D41. I would like to tender it as D41A and the translation as D41B, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. We do not have the 28 translation, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: B is the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: B is the English translation, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection. Defence Exhibit 41A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to explain the translations were ready only at a very late stage. That is the reason why there might be some difficulties in providing the Prosecution with the translations, although the original ones have been presented to them earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is fine. Maybe at the recess at 4.00 you have some English translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we will give them to the Prosecution. Perhaps, Professor Hayden, could you explain whether in this Exhibit these nationalist thoughts have been reflected in this constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. Let me say that you can see the date on the document. On the translation it says 17th July 1989, and these are proposed draft amendments to the constitution of Slovenia. This was done because the federal constitution had a clause that said that Republican constitutions could not be contrary to the federal constitution, unless when the federal constitution was amended it became necessary to amend the Republican constitutions, all of which had contained the socialist self-management structures that had now been taken out of the federal constitution. This was part of the process of amending the Slovenian 28 constitution. What we have here is several aspects of these amendments, and I think we will cover some of them later, that could be seen as nationalistic, but part of what is interesting here is this amendment 43(C) as presented in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have that on the screen, if possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a very curious provision at the time that it was introduced. You see, it refers to the Italian and Hungarian minorities as autochthonous, if I pronounce that correctly, autochthonous minorities. In the late 1980s in Slovenia, the idea of nationalism, that Slovenia should be a state for Slovenes, often took the form of expressions of hostility to the roughly 12 or 14 per cent of population of Slovenia who were not ethnic Slovenes and who were from other parts of the former Yugoslavia. Politely, they were referred to by the German term of Gastarbajteri, gas workers, or as southerners, Juznjaci. There were much less complimentary terms used for them. You might regard it as being comparable in many ways to the types of disparaging comments that are made about Turks, for example, in Germany. It was very curious when the Slovenes amended their constitution that they would suddenly proclaim autochthonous minorities. This was a phrase that was certainly new to Yugoslav constitutional discourse to proclaim a group of people to be autochthonous minorities and, on that grounds, to guarantee them the right freely to use their language, express and develop their natural culture, etc. etc. 28 This document, as you see, goes on and there are justifications about this. What is interesting about it is that by distinguishing between the autochthonous minorities and other minorities within Slovenia, this provision seemed to give superior rights to these autochthonous minorities to the detriment of minorities who were not of the Italian and Hungarian groups. I should say that, in terms of numbers, the Italian and Hungarian minorities in Slovenia are (and were in 1989 and are now) of minimal importance. You are talking, I do not know, perhaps 20,000 or maybe 30,000 people out of a population of approximately 2 million. So that there was a great deal of symbolism involved in this. It was thus interpreted by the members of other Yugoslav nations living in Slovenia, not Slovenes and not Italian and Hungarian autochthonous minorities. It suddenly seemed to be put in a rather ambiguous and anomalous, in terms of the federal constitution, provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you say that this was not in concordance with the federal constitution and could you explain that more precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly the federal constitution, if you recall, there was Article, was it, 249 that said that citizens of one Republic on the territory of another Republic would have equal rights to the citizens of that Republic. You did have these equal protection clauses, and this seemed to be brought into question by the political discourse going on in Slovenia at the time which was, frankly, growing increasingly hostile to non-Slovenes, and by this sudden constitutional effort to 28 privilege the minimal autochthonous minorities as composed -- I am sorry, as compared with whom, well, as compared with the other non-Slovenes in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, you earlier referred to Article 246. In your reference you just made to 249. Was this a mistake or did you really intend to refer to another Article than you did before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I would have to bring back Exhibit 19 and clarify it, but I was referring to the Article, the second Article, that I read under equal protection, the one that dealt primarily with citizenship, but that also said -- we had both Articles, we had an equal protection clause and that is 154 and then we had -- it has been my professional misfortune to have to deal with the two longest constitutions in the world, that of Yugoslavia and that of India, both of which were amended many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The question was 246 or 249?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He said 249.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: He said 249, but his earlier reference was 246, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, 246, I may well have referred to (or should have) because 246 which is, fortunately, on the same page or facing, referring to "... the languages of the nations and nationalities and their alphabet shall be equal throughout the territory of Yugoslavia". This principle on the equality of languages, and then we have 249: "Citizens of Republics shall on the territory of another Republic" ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You might have a different idea of speed, Professor Hayden, but I have some difficulties in following you when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. OK. 246 is, I believe, relevant because it does 28 refer to a provision for equality of the languages and alphabets of the nations and nationalities as being equal throughout the territory of Yugoslavia. We may see a bit later that some of the Slovenian amendments had to do -- potentially violated this provision as well. Then, of course, Article 249, that "Citizens of a Republic shall on the territory of another Republic have the same rights and duties as the citizens of that Republic". This seemed to be brought into question in Slovenia with the arrival of this amendment, 43(C).

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One of our French interpreters is from [Redacted] so I know that he is keeping up with the witness, unless he is having a problem with his northern accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this Exhibit is, what this document is, Professor Hayden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In which language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in Serbo-Croatian or Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a translation attached to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a constitution -- there is a translation accompanying it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid I gave you all four or five copies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You gave me everything, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Would you just take the original text and the translation and please return the other ones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, there is a translation, the 28 constitution -- well, this is from a volume that was simply the collected constitutions of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Republics and of the autonomous provinces. It was published in Belgrade in 1974. We have a translation of Article 1 of the constitution of Croatia of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document as Exhibit 42A for the original language and B for the translation of Article 1, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have 42B yet, the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we do not have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Usher, would you come, please, and pick up one of the English translations? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to present another document to you. It is in the English language, so no problem with translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection? Defence Exhibit 42A and B will be admitted.
