utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you tell us what document this is in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. This is the preamble and the first four Articles of the constitution of Croatia of 1990. It comes from a volume published by the Parliament of the Republic of Croatia, the Sabor, that I obtained in Zagreb from officials of the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour, as Exhibit 43, 28 Defence Exhibit 43.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 43 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you explain to us, reading these Articles, how the 1974 constitution of Croatia was changed in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at Article 1 of the 1974 constitution ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will see the -- do you have it -- you see the normal rhetoric of Yugoslav constitutions in 1974 at the time of self-management socialism: "The Socialist Republic of Croatia is a state based on the sovereignty of the people, the authority and self-management of the worker class and all working people, is a socialist self-management democratic community of working people and citizens in equal nations and nationalities". The next line is of interest. It says: "The Socialist Republic of Croatia is a national state of the Croatian people" -- and "Croatian people", this is a translation of "Hrvatski", which is Croat, "Narod", a term that I have discussed earlier -- "a state of the Serbian people in Croatia and a state of the nationalities living within it". This formation recognises the importance to the Serbs of Croatia, who were the largest group in Croatia who were not ethnic Croats, and who regarded themselves or wished to be regarded as having a status equal to that of Croats in a political sense. So they are included here ahead of the 28 nationalities. This also reflects the Yugoslav structure at the time between the state forming nations, the narodi, narods -- if I can put an English plural on a Serbo-Croatian word -- and the narodnosti, the nationalities, and it is clear that, constitutionally, the narodi, narods, are privileged in a sense, political sense, over the nationalities. If we would look at the next document, the constitution of the Republic of Croatia of 1990, I should say that immediately after taking power in 1990, the frankly nationalist Croatian government that was elected in 1990, the government of the Croatian Democratic Union, or HDZ (as I think it has been identified in documents here), amended the constitution to put Serbs on the level of the other minorities. That was in, I believe, June or July of 1990, but since a whole constitution was passed in December 1990, it brought a new constitution. This preamble is rather interesting. It is the longest preamble, I think, in the Republics of the former Yugoslavia. It is an interesting history lesson that also establishes the identity of the state. If you look at these historical foundations, the milliennia national identity of the Croatian nation, Hrvatski narod, Croat narod, continuity of its statehood, if you read down this, these historical foundations had to do with the Croat nation. If I may remove it for a minute, it is a little hard to -- right, it figures, it is at the bottom of the page which barely fits here. OK. The last paragraph here, "Proceeding 28 from the above presented historical" -- well, look in the paragraph above that: "The historic turn point marked by the rejection of the communist system and changes in the international order in Europe, the Croatian nation" -- this is the narod, this is Hrvatski narod, "reaffirmed at the first democratic elections by its freely expressed will" -- this is the will of the Croatian nation, the Croat narod -- "its millennia statehood and resolution to establish the Republic of Croatia as a sovereign state", and then: "Proceeding from the above presented historical facts, in referring to the right of the Croatian nation, Hrvatski narod, Croat narod, to self-determination in state sovereignty, the Republic of Croatia is hereby established as the national state of the Croatian nation and a state of members of other nations" -- going down the page -- "and minorities who are citizens, Serbs, Muslims, Slovenes" etc. and others "who are guaranteed equality with citizens". But this was considered to be an important symbolic change. The preambles in these constitutions have enormous symbolic value. Even though lawyers tend to regard preambles as not been being in the operative parts of constitutions, they have enormous symbolic value. One of the ways that you see this, of course, is that the right to self-determination in the Yugoslav federal constitution of 1974 (which was discussed when Dr. Gow testified) was mentioned only in the preamble. It was not part of the operative sections of the constitution, but it had enormous symbolic value. There is a great deal of symbolic 28 value here in taking the Serbs from a position that is a bit in front spatially and politically of the minorities in putting them into this same rung.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to present another document to you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That preamble also noted that there was a right of secession. Are you going to talk about that at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I certainly can. You see this being asserted in the Croatian constitution. Yes, it is at the bottom of the left-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid that you are now quoting from the document that has just been given to you -- no, sorry. I am mistaken, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am referring to the Republic of Croatia. Yes, including "the inviolable right to secession and association". The association here was taken to mean association with other nations. That is what "association" here means. Yes, this is being proclaimed in the Croatian constitution. Now, remember, in the federal constitution it is a very disputed issue because the right to secession is mentioned only in the preamble, and in the operative part there is a provision that says that the external borders of Yugoslavia could be changed only with the unanimous consent of all the republics. So, is this in accordance with the federal constitution? Well, it is hard to tell, but I think when we are looking at these preamables we are looking at symbolic statements that in many ways overtake in importance the 28 operative parts of the constitutions themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, if you would look at the document I just presented to you, could you first tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a copy of one page in an American journal called "Problems of Post Communism", page 26 of the edition of September/October 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 44, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not have it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 44 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, without going through the whole left part of the page, could you please tell us what it represents, what it contains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. I should say that this is actually a page from an article of mine that was supposed to appear on 1st September and had not appeared, and so that this was actually sent to me by the publisher at my request. What we are interested in are the materials in the box on the left-hand side of the page and these are -- are we OK?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I indicated I did not have a copy of it. Your Honour, in due course might the Defence provide us with the entire article rather than just the page?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think so. You should provide them with the entire article. But it is two minutes before 4.00, we normally recess at 4.00, so we will recess now and, Mr. Orie, would you 28 provide the Prosecution, please, with a copy of all of the Exhibits that you intend to offer to this witness, if you have them? If they are just missing the English translation, give them that, but if you are going to offer one page of an article, they should have the entire article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, specifically I will try to have all documents in full detail. This is, as a matter of fact, just, I do not know how to say it in English, it is just quoting from several constitutions, a survey. I will not go into the text of the article, but I will just refer to that part that gives quotations of all constitutions of the Republics rather than going into the line of reasoning in the article.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you are going to use a part of a document, it seems to me that the opposing side is entitled to the entire document. I do not think it should be a problem. I am sure Professor Hayden has it with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, your Honour, I am afraid I do not. This was the problem. I had sent back the page proofs. They had assured me that the issue would appear. The issue did not appear. All that I am going to discuss -- I use this because it put in one easily accessible place the preambles to the constitutions. So, literally, all we are going to discuss are these constitutional excerpts. We are not going to discuss the insides of the page which I wrote and it will not be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In that event, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection. Exhibit 44 will be admitted and we will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor Hayden, after having pointed out to us that this nationalist tendency was reflected in the amendment to the Slovenian constitution and the amendments to the Croatian constitution, could you please put on the screen the document I just gave to you -- you said it was an article of yours that has not yet been published -- and explain to us, perhaps, by pointing to a few examples, what is on the left-hand side of that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. What I have done here is make a selection of the text from the current constitutions or, at least, at the time that I wrote the article they were current, excerpts from the constitutions of the post Yugoslav republics, looking at the formulation of whose state it is. You will see there is a common pattern. Again we can see with Croatia, the inalienable right to self-determination and state sovereignty of the Croatian nation, Hrvatski narod. Macedonia refers to the heritage of the Macedonian nation and their struggle for the creation of their own state. Montenegro, the right of the Montenegrin nation to its own state. Serbia, the struggle of the Serbian nation for independence and the determination to establish a democratic state of the Serbian nation. It continues. You see similar formulations for Slovenia, the right of Slovene nation to self-determination and the fact that they have established their 28 own statehood. Finally, the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the 1991 constitution, referring to the right of the Serbian nation to self-determination and establish a democratic state of the Serbian nation on its own historical and ethnic space, and a similar formulation in the Republika Srpske or Serbian Republic from 1992. So, there is a pattern here consistently in these constitutions. The formulation is that the state belongs to the narod, which is, in American terms, an ethnic group. This is a formulation that may seem symbolic and in most or if not all of these constitutions there are passages in the operative parts that refer to equal rights etc. However, if you could envision a situation in which the preamble of the American constitution would be amended so that instead of reading "We, the people of the United States", it were to read "We, the white protestant people of the United States", or the constitution of India to be amended so that the preamble would read, instead of "We, the people of India", it would read, "We, the Hindu people of India", and imagine the interpretations that would be given to an equal rights clause by governments that would make such a change, I think you may have a better grasp of the symbolism involved in these constitution formulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I do not see the Bosnia-Herzegovina, we might go into that later perhaps more in detail, but I do not see it in there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina in this regard has to 28 do with the nature of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In all of these other examples, you do have a majority narod in Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, but in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no majority narod. By 1991, the largest group were the Muslims and Muslim here is a narod. It is not simply a religious affiliation. It is a narod in Yugoslav terms. 44 per cent followed by Serbs as, I think, 31, Croats at 17, Yugoslavs and others. So there is no majority narod here to whom you can assign sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will go into that perhaps later on in more detail, Professor Hayden.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question, please, regarding this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say Muslim is a narod, but then you describe "narod" as "given birth to". Earlier you said that, for example, people who were given birth to in Serbia would considered themselves Serbian; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not quite so, your Honour, because one may be an ethnic Serb, no matter where one is born. I mean, one may be an ethnic Serb and be born in Chicago or Botswana, if one is born to Serbian parents and, specifically, a Serbian father.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Meaning a father born in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, meaning a father who is, in American terms, an ethnic Serb. This is ascribed identity, just as one may be an ethnic German, of ethnic German parentage, in Romanija for 500 years, a group in Romanija called Saxons, or Germans in Solezia(?) in Poland. 28 This European concept of nation is a bit different from the American concept and it makes it a bit hard to talk about. Just if I can try one more example: We now have in Germany the second, third, maybe even fourth, generation of Turks who are born -- maybe born in Germany, may in fact be monolingual speakers of German, but are not considered by the German to be German. They are considered to be Turks. In Yugoslav terms, they would be members of the Turkish narod, as opposed to the German narod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But "narod" means nation, occasionally a people, but most closely to the verb meaning "to give birth". So that if Muslim is narod, you say that Muslim is a narod, how can you determine that then? Were not the Muslims given a state earlier and is that a possible way to consider Muslims as an ethnic group as opposed to a religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The religion in this case identifies the ethnic group. This is not unusual in Yugoslavia. In fact, by now the definitive division between Serbs and Croats is that Serbs are orthodox Christians. One does not have to be a believer, of course. I mean, if your parents are Serbs, you are a Serb. If your parents are Muslim, you are a Muslim. Whether or not you go to church or go to the mosque is really irrelevant. This is an ascribed status. It is not unique in the former Yugoslavia. Muslim as an ethnic group in this sense could be found, for example, in Sri Lanka with a largest group are Sinhalise followed by Tamils, but there is a group of Muslims who are actually speakers of Tamil, but are not regarded by the Tamils 28 as being Tamil. The population that speaks what I learned as Serbo-Croatian is divided among Serbs, Croats and Muslims primarily and these are, in American terms, ethnic groups. The Muslims as a narod did not have that constitutional status until 1971, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The constitutional status then came from what, the fact that they were recognised as a state in a constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were recognised as a constituent nation, as one of the narodi of Yugoslavia. This is a Yugoslav constitutional distinction that I think Professor Gow also talked about. It is the distinction between the narodi, narods, and narodnosti, nationalities. The narods are the groups, the Serbs, Croats, and after '71 Muslims, Slovenes, Montenegrins, Macedonians, who are the state-forming people. The narodnosti are minorities whose, if you will, mother state or the state of their narod group is another state. Hungary, for example; the Hungarian minority in Serbia or in Slovenia would be a narodnos because there is a Hungarian state. Much of central Europe has to grapple with these questions of having what are, in Yugoslav terms, narod, denarods and narodnosti, and some of the tensions in central Europe come from this. For example, several years ago the President of Hungary said that he was not only President of Hungary, he was President of all Hungarians. Well, there are a substantial number of Hungarians in Romanija and the Romanijan government was not overly pleased with this pronouncement by the President 28 of Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for asking so many questions. I guess, Professor Hayden, you have come to testify after so many months and we have heard testimony about whether it is religion or ethnicity. There has been some literature to suggest that all are the same ethnicity, that is, Slavs. But I think that what you are saying is that it is a state-forming people, at least narod, and in that respect you can consider Muslims to be a separate ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so and, of course, they all consider themselves to be of these groups. As I say, one is born into this group, and whether or not one is a practising Muslim or believing Muslim is absolutely irrelevant to one's identity as a member of the Muslim narod. Obviously, questions arise when you have mixed marriages and those questions do arise. That is also in many ways a quite modern phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you a question? I do not know whether you know the answer to this. But, identification cards, do they customarily or did they customarily in 1990, for instance, indicate the particular ethnic group or narod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that the identification cards at that time did so. You will see later that, however, in Bosnia and Herzegovina the status of narod was extremely important in a constitutional sense, so that the candidates for the elections in Bosnia in 1990 were all identified by their status as narod. I should say that one would declare this. You could declare -- you would declare your own identity at the time of 28 the census, for example. So that you could declare yourself to be a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim or a Yugoslav, and it was these self-ascribed identities that were listed in the Bosnian elections in 1990. But, as you will see later, these identifications have constitutional importance in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then following that up, if someone had no religious beliefs, as certainly was the case with a number of the population of Yugoslavia in 1990, was there any difficulty at all in transforming yourself from a Muslim to a Serb, assuming that you were moving to a different part of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the language would be identical, in every respect you would appear to be one of an undifferentiated mass, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily exactly. For one thing, personal names are often indicative. In terms of languages, dialects of any language are primarily regional, so that everyone from Sarajevo would speak a Sarajevo dialect, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, you would be identified as a Bosnian. But it would have been unlikely that one would take, if one were a Muslim, that one would then present oneself as a Serb. It would be much more likely that if one did not feel oneself to be a Muslim that you would take the -- proclaim the identity of Yugoslav. In fact, this was one of the options on the census forms and the number of self-identified Yugoslavs rose through the census of 1981 and then dropped dramatically in the census taken at the beginning of April in 1991 when it suddenly did not seem very wise to declare oneself as a Yugoslav. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then what of Bosniacs? If you were a Muslim, it was fashionable to call yourself Bosniac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, no, and you will see in the materials that will be presented later, which is an excerpt from the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the identification of the candidates for elections -- can I talk about this, if it has not been presented?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know. It is up to -- Mr. Orie does not seem to mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We will present it later. It is simply that you will see ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will get to it later if you want, I do not know, but answer Judge Stephen's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The identification would be Serb or Yugoslav or Croat or Muslim. The term "Bosniac" did not come into common use until 1994. It is actually an older term. It is an English pronunciation of the word Bosnjak, which was a term coined in the Austro-Hungarian Empire in an attempt to provide an identity for the residents of Bosnia that would not differentiate them, that all of them could call themselves Bosnjaci. Bosnjak is the singular, Bosnjaci is the plural. It never caught on. You can refer to someone from Bosnia as a Bosanac as opposed to Bosnjak, you see? If I am speaking Serbo-Croatian, I refer to someone from Bosnia, I will say, "He is a Bosanac", and that can be anyone from Bosnia. You can tell by the accent, for example. But Bosniac was not used until the time of the -- essentially, the time that the United States crafted the 28 Croat/Muslim federation in March of 1974 (sic), and rather than call it the federation of Croats and Muslims, they used the term "Bosniac" Bosniacs. I do not think that the term has got great currency amongst the people of Bosnia themselves. I just had a student returned from there, and one of her assignment was to see if people were calling themselves "Bosniacs"; they are not, but it is a political label that is very useful to identify this population, but if you refer to "Bosniacs", they are Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may just an additional question? You have just referred to 1974 as a time when the federation of Croats and Muslims was ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I say 74?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, 94. It was 1994. I misspoke. It is called the Washington Agreement and it was the -- it was signed in Washington in March of 1994. If I said '74, it was a pure misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that. Professor Hayden, I would like to present to you another document. Could you explain to us, first, what it is before I tender it as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a copy of an article from the journal Radio Free Europe Radio Liberty Research Report published at that time in Munich, Germany, by Radio Free Europe Radio Liberty. It is by an analyst who worked and I think still works there called Stan Markotich and it is called "Ethnic Serbs in Tudjman's Croatia". It is dated 24 September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour, as Defence Exhibit 28 45A because I will tender another document that is closely linked to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 45A will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, does this document reflect the opinion of Dr. Tudjman, President of Croatia at that time, about the new constitutional situation in Croatia? If you refer to parts of the article, would you please then put them on the overhead projector so that we all can follow you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that I can follow it. OK. In the article, and this is only part of the article that I will actually refer to, it is not the words of Mr. Markotich, although he did translate them, he included in this article an excerpt from a speech by Franjo Tudjman, President of Croatia, the President who was elected in 1990 and whose government immediately amended the Croatian constitution. If you can see the quote there on page 30, I believe, of the article which is now on the screen, these are the words of President Tudjman and says: "The Serbs in Croatia cannot become a ruling people. We have arranged our affairs in democratic Croatia the way the Serbs in Serbia, the Slovenes in Slovenia, the Macedonians in Macedonia and every people the world over have arranged their affairs. Here in Croatia the Croatians are sovereign", and I will say that I checked the original and he says "Hrvatski narod", the Croat nation, is sovereign, "and to the Serbs are accorded all the rights of a national minority and all 28 individual rights, but it cannot be asked that about eight per cent of the population, the Serbs, who found themselves here as a result of historical developments should be sovereign in the country of Croatia because nowhere in the world could such an arrangement exist". Now, the formulation, and he identifies it, as have I, in the boxed text -- I have forgotten the Exhibit, 44, that had the various constitutional excerpts -- he clearly identifies who is sovereign and you will see that the Serbs are excluded from the sovereign body in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like to present another document to you in relation to your remark that you checked your original language. (Handed) Could you tell us what this document is and what it contains in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a photocopy of an article from the Croatian News weekly magazine, Danas, from June, and I do not know if it is June or not, I cannot quite read it, it is the 2nd of something, 1993. This is actually the article that was used as a source by Mr. Markotich for the quote by Franjo Tudjman that I just read. I did not do this translation; Markotich did and so I wanted to check the original and the original is contained here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender that document as Exhibit 45B, your Honour. I am aware that it is not a full document but it is only the quote that I would like to refer to and Professor Hayden ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The complete article is there. The article in the magazine was only two pages. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 45B?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 45B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, is there a translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why, it is the quote that was in the English text and of which Professor Hayden has told us that he verified it in the original language. Therefore, I provided also an article giving the original language of this quote. Professor Hayden, having gone through all these amendments to the constitutions of the republics, more in detail the Slovenian constitution, the Croatian constitution and the opinion about sovereignty by Dr. Tudjman, could you tell us whether the western world -- I am referring especially to the European Union and the United States -- did interpret these developments correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say not. The position of the western world and the United States, the European Community in particular, ignored these formulations of sovereignty, of whose state it is, quite a lot, virtually entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, formulations -- the position of the western world that it was republics that had the right to secede was flatly in contradiction to what these Yugoslav politicians were telling their own people. For example, the extract from the 1990 Croatian constitution clearly referred to the right of the Croat nation to secede as, of course, the constitution of Yugoslavia of 1974 in its reference to secession, which was only in the 28 preamble, had referred to the right of the narodi, narods, to secede, not of the republics. So that the politics of the nationalist movements within Yugoslavia were based on the premise of creating the state, the territory and the government belonging to the narod, and not in any sense a body of undifferentiated citizens. The position of the western world that what was at stake was the right, as I think the German government put it, a limited right, to self-determination, meaning the right of the citizens within the borders of the existing Yugoslav republics to determine whether they would secede was a reasoning that was at flat variance with that of the Yugoslav political leaders themselves and the constructions that had, in fact, won in 1990, and that drove the political movements. The formulation of the western world seemed premised on a policy of equal citizens. The political movements that have succeeded in Yugoslavia with the free and fair elections of 1990 have not posited polities of equal citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Hayden. I would like to go now to a different subject. I would like to speak with you about the dismantling of the Yugoslav Federation. I would like to be shown to you Exhibit 21 before I put any questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, let me ask one more question. If you say that the federal constitution of 1974 recognised the right of narods ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Narod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- to secede but did not speak in terms of republics, that they 28 spoke in terms of narods ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: --- then the various constitutions of the Republics in 1990 identified themselves as states consisting of narods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, narods and others, but the narod, the majority narod, is sovereign in the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Exactly. We have seen, at least, the Croatian preamble allowed for a right to secede. Then if you put the two together, would you say that the 1974 federal constitution, if read together with the 1990 Republic, the constitutions of the various republics, would allow for the right of secession? Do you understand what I am trying to ask? I may have it confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I do, but the question is to whom does the right belong? Does it belong to the Republic or does it belong to the narod? Actually, the Croatian constitution of 1990 is consistent with a preamble of the federal constitution of 1974 by giving the right to secession to the narod, not to the Republic, but to the narod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What does it say about who the state consists of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The 1990 constitution, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 1990 constitution defines Croatia. It justifies Croatia on the basis of ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- the Croatian people, yes, but there are others in Croatia. This is the problem. There were more others in Croatia then than there are now. The problem here is that none of the 28 Yugoslav republics were homogenous, even in Slovenia which was generally regarded as the most homogenous, by the 1991 census, I think, 14 per cent of the population were not ethnic Slovenes. In Serbia, about 65 per cent of the population are ethnic Serbs. This is the problem that I know was going through in Dr. Gow's testimony, that the Yugoslav constitutional structures of 1974 referred to -- as I said, they had the dual sovereignty of the narods and the workers. When that is removed, you have only the narods, but here you have a problem because then the Republican constitutions give superior rights within each Republic to the one narod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Republican constitutions may be wrong by saying in the preamble that it is a state consisting of Croatian people, but they make that judgment, whoever was able to write the constitution. If they say that, right or wrong, but if they say that, and then you read that together with the federal constitution, would it not be reasonable for a Croatian reading this preamble to say: "Well, our preamble says that we are a state of Croatian people, a narod, a Croatian people. The 1974 federal constitution allows for secession of narods. Thus, we can secede". They were wrong, you would say, in their preamble in 1990 saying that it was a state of Croatian people, because there were many, many other people in significant minorities in terms of numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a practical matter, it is likely to work that way in a state where you have a pronounced majority narod. Your problems come 28 in the portions of states where, for example, one of the minorities is a local majority and say, "We are a narod, we have the right to secede", or in Bosnia and Herzegovina where there is no majority narod and where, for example, where the Croats of western Herzegovina, for example, proclaimed their own mini state within Bosnia and Herzegovina on the grounds of the right to self-determination and self-determination of the narod, which is the constitutional structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I thought that in those excerpts from most, but not all because Bosnia-Herzegovina was not included, of the republics there was a careful inclusion in the statement of who the people were, not only of the majority narod but also of others that was recognised, and they were recognised as being citizens, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Citizens but not part of the sovereign body which is -- well, it is not a state of equal citizens. There may be citizens of the state, but they are not part of the sovereign body. If one reads the speeches and the position and papers of the various political leaders, they are very clear about this. This is not a type of structure that we are used to thinking about, because we would like to posit a polity of equal citizens. This is the modern meaning of democracy. Here, though, only one part of the citizenry is sovereign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Although that does not in fact emerge, does it, from those small portions that you quote? You have to look at what the leaders say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is true. I find the formulation, though, in the preambles 28 of the constitution to be extremely indicative of what it is all about and then prefer Dr. Tudjman's speech to actually state the point perhaps more clearly than I have. I might draw a rather different parallel. The point of the socialist state was to serve, to represent, not the entire population, but only part of the population, the working class and the working people, which is what the state is there for constitutionally defined, legally implemented. What succeeded state socialism in the former Yugoslav Republics was another form of a state in which the state is there, constitutionally defined and legally implemented, to serve one part of the population and that is the majority narod.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As you said, if we had a constitution which said, "We, the white Protestant", cross out even males ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could be that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: "in order to form a more perfect union."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then you go on to mention some other people, you wonder who are the narods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Particularly when the amendment is made from the all-inclusive "we, the people" and then suddenly amendments are inserted that say, "We, the white Protestant male people and others.".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, you say you have listed this witness for two days and if this continues -- so we will be quiet. I will be quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think we will manage, your Honour. I am still 28 optimistic that we will manage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have heard so much testimony. Obviously, as we have said, we have read through these transcripts and we are now at the point of trying to resolve in our minds some questions. One of them had to do with ethnicity. Unfortunately, Professor Hayden, you came ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will tell you that I will not cover in the testimony of Dr. Hayden questions concerning all the issues dealt with by Dr. Gow. So we will concentrate on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, could you please have a look at Exhibit 21 that is presented to you, as I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am holding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what you understand it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is a photocopy of the memorandum, the famous memorandum, of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts of 1986. It is from the Zagreb magazine Nase Teme from 1989 and it has attached a translation, it has attached an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow has testified on this memorandum. Could you please tell us whether this memorandum was unique to Serbia, such a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The memorandum discusses the problems of the Serbs in Yugoslavia, and as a document discussing the problems of one of the nations of Yugoslavia the memorandum was certainly not unique at the time that it was written and not published. It 28 was never adopted by the Serbian Academy, and in fact it was not published until it was pirated into a Zagreb magazine, a Croatian magazine in 1989, but it was by no means the only such document in Yugoslavia in the late 80s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it was not the only document, this memorandum, could you point to similar documents that have been prepared and discussed elsewhere within the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The primary document that I would think of would be something called the Slovenian National Programme which was a set of articles drafted by Slovenian intellectuals in approximately 1986/87, in other words at the same time that the group of -- they were literally identified on the cover as a group of intellectuals of the Serbian Academy. The Slovenian National Programme was published in Slovenia in a journal called Nova Revija, New Review, in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us have you ever seen that document, the Slovenian National Programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen the document, yes, I have held the document, yes, when I was in Slovenia in 1989. It was a magazine that had been openly for sale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it was published in the magazine Nova Revija, New Review, which was a magazine which I think itself came into existence in the 1980s in Slovenia and was, essentially, the magazine of Slovenian nationalist intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, did you obtain a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At the time when I was in Slovenia in 1989 I saw it at a 28 friend's home. My friend had it. I could see it, but I was not able to acquire a copy then. I have to say I did not, it did not occur to me, well, it occurred to me but making a copy then of the entire journal, I figured I would get it elsewhere. Making photocopies in Yugoslavia at that time was expensive and I thought I would get it, but I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to present to you another document, Professor Hayden, because I would like to ask you some questions on whether this document really existed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of actually two articles that appeared in consecutive issues of a weekly newspaper in Belgrade called Nedeljni Telegraph or Weekly Telegraph, the issue of 24th July 1996, the issue of 31 July 1996. It is an article about a meeting between Serbian intellectuals and Slovenian intellectuals in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- unfortunately, your Honour, we have not been able to have a translation made of this document. First I tender this document as an Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be 46?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That will be 46, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection? It is only in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you asking the witness to read a portion of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will ask the witness to read portions of it. The main reason why I am doing this is since we cannot present, as you have heard, Slovenian National Programme, I would like to 28 establish that this document did exist and some support of the memory of Professor Hayden as to the existence and the content of the document he saw at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, 46 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should say that I had first heard of the meeting of Serbian intellectuals and Slovene intellectuals that is reported in this document from Professor Markotic who is listed as author and whose picture is on the front page. I heard about this from him in a conversation that I had with him in January 1991 in Belgrade five years ago and six years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please point at the relevant parts of this article, and perhaps read slowly those parts that are referring to this movement, this meeting, and this Slovenian National Programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was this given to the translators as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We have given the relevant parts to the translators in order to facilitate a quick translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I would like to do is read several passages from here. I prepared myself a photocopy in which I marked the passages so that I could find them easily. I believe that a similar copy was given to the translators so that they would be able to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you could perhaps also indicate those parts on the overhead projector where the original Exhibit is. 28

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Starting here with the words Slovenci, and I am afraid the translators will have to put up with my accent in Serbo-Croatian, but then you will listen to the translation instead of me and you will be better off. For the translators this would be the excerpt marked No. 1 on the copy they have. [In translation] "Today the Slovenians feel that the idea of belonging of Slovenes in Yugoslavia is dead or if nothing else dying. People feel disappointed and disillusioned and deceived in their expectations. We have nothing to expect any longer. We do not feel that we are in our own country. As a state product Yugoslavia is dead in the minds of the people." The speaker is Bucar, later the President of the Slovenian National Assembly. If we go further down the page, and there is no real easy way to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could get some help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have to show it on the screen as well as read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think perhaps it is easier, especially since Dr. Gow is there, if you indicate what part you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. The speaker is still Bucar and where my finger is -- yes, beginning with the words -- the pointer is on it. Can you get it over to there. I see it but I do not see the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You should perhaps move the document a bit so that the pointer is in the picture as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is right here beginning with the word "Yesu" which is still not on here. 28

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you put your highlighted copy on the overhead and then turn, if they will turn that towards you, Mr. Usher, see if you can turn it over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We want passage No. 2.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can turn the elmo towards the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. It is the point marked No. 2 and outlined and highlighted in pink. Again I think the speaker is Bucar. [ In translation] "Are the Serbs nationalists? If they are, good for them. Unfortunately, there is a major difference between the Slovenians and Serbs as nationalists. To our mind, the idea of Yugoslav-hood is of secondary importance. To you it is of primary importance. We want autonomy and for you Yugoslavia has been and still is the road to the solution of the Serb question. What interest could we have in common then?" No. 3, the speaker here is Yanez Urbancic with whom I am not actually familiar. [In translation] "The fundamental thing for me is that I am a Slovene, that I love my people and my language, and I want to remain that. I have no visions about future Yugoslavia. The most important thing is that this fundamental national identity of mine ought to be inviolate and respected in it." From the second article -- no, I missed one. Again, I am sorry, we have not had these translated. The Translation Service was not able to do this. I would like to see four. I believe the speaker is still Urbancic. This is again No. 4. [In translation] "Nevertheless, the principal 28 contradiction between the view that the people with a fatherland is the vital thing and the universalists or even Marxist theory that there are more important things from the national determination. A whole movement has two meanings. On the one hand, integration of Europe includes universalism. On the other, on the opposite side is the movement for the manifestation of national rights. Nonetheless, the people cannot be a tool of anything else, socialism, communism. A people is a means, a purpose unto itself." From the second article 31 July, the speaker here is Tone Hribar who, as I recall, was editor of Nova Revija. Perhaps I should explain here because he makes a reference to something called the Yavnosti. Yavnost was supposed to be a magazine in Serbia that was going to be begun by opposition intellectuals, opposition to the regime, the Communist regime, and it was not in fact begun. The state did not permit it to exist, but the comparison here is between Nova Revija, the Slovenian journal, and Yavnosti, the Serbian one that was going to be initiated by the Serbian participants in this discussion. [In translation] "I need to say that the initiative to start Nova Revija was started here as early as 1980, slightly before Yavnost. Yavnost attempted to be a Yugoslav journal and we thought that it ought first to assert itself as a Serb journal and then the integration could come about." Just a couple more, if you will bear with me. The speaker in No. 5 is Taras Kermaner who was and is a Slovenian writer. [In translation] "How different it is with Serbs for 28 whom Yugoslav is an objective interest and need because they are torn and discordant. If Yugoslavia were to break apart Serbs would lose almost half of the population." This is Yugoslavia in World War II (?) [In translation] "Avner (?) Yugoslavia promoted brotherhood and unity which was a substitute for the autonomy and civil society, but brotherhood always means terror and demagogy and unity means homogenization". I should add that "Bretsvo Jedicstvo" brotherhood and unity, was one of the primary ideological bases of the Yugoslavia that existed under Tito and until 1991. The constitution of 1974 makes fairly frequent references to Bretsvo Jedicstvo, brotherhood and unity. Finally, the speaker is again France Bucar. [In translation] "The Serbs need to follow their own national interest. We are for confederalism. However, the solution to the problem is not within the categories of federalism or confederalism. I respect your nationalism but it comes into conflict with the Slovenian national concept." Thank you. As I said, these intellectuals, among others, wrote a Slovenian national programme that was published in Nova Revija in 1987, as it indicates here. Bucar had a certain political success in Slovenia later. I can say that other contributors to Nova Revija also had political success in the elections in 1990 in the victory of the nationalist coalition that won then and has governed the governments of Slovenia since 1990. 28

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Heyden, do I understand well that this political language was used far before the memorandum was drafted, the memorandum which was Exhibit 21?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this meeting took place in 1985 and the memorandum was written or begun in 1986. I also remember that one of the people whose words I read here, Taras Kermaner, had quite shocked the Serbian intellectual public in I think it was the summer of 1985 or 1986 with a so-called "letter to my Serbian friend" first published in Slovenia and then republished in Serbia. That was very much of an anti-Yugoslav polemic and in many ways an anti-Serbian one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, I would like you to be shown now Prosecution Exhibit 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think I should say that I do not follow at all what all this comes to. Perhaps I am not intended to at this stage, but to me it is meaningless the last 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to explain to you what it is all about. A lot of attention has been paid by the Prosecutor to sovereignty, the right to secession, where it all started. What the Defence intends to do is to give a different picture, first of all, to clarify a few constitutional issues, then to make clear that the statement of Dr. Gow, that it all started -- and that is one of my next questions -- were compared and the conclusions drawn by Dr. Gow, especially from Exhibit 24, confront this witness with it and see if he comes to the same conclusion, the main conclusion of Dr. Gow being that this nationalistic movement mainly arose in Serbia, in the Belgrade 28 areas, and to see whether this is also the opinion of Professor Hayden. The relevance of it I think stems from the relevance attached to it by the Prosecution. That is the reason why we do not want to have it unanswered, and the relevance for the whole case of course still has to be considered later on. Professor Hayden, Exhibit 24, could you please bring into our mind what Exhibit 24 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24 is an English translation of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to take you to a part which, as I understand, is not exactly the text of the constitution itself, on pages 10, 11, small numbers, which is a part written, as far as I understand, by a certain Mr. Markotich.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please give your comment on that part, the last part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Referring to the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says: "Due to the present constitutional status of Serbia, the question may arise as to whether Serbia with the new constitution has turned its back to the Federal Yugoslavia. By the new constitution Serbia has only made more precise the character of its link with Yugoslavia. Serbia has entirely recognised the primacy of the federal constitution until Yugoslavia continues to have the federal order." I suspect the translation is wrong and it should have said, "while Yugoslavia continues to have a federal order". "Some other non-Federal Yugoslavia is beyond the political and state interest of Serbia 28 precisely because of that and due to the tendency of squandering the Federal Yugoslavia" which is now visible "Serbia had to include in its constitution the 'defensive clause' to a violation of the federal constitution that the detriment of Serbia entitles Serbia to self-defence in such cases, namely, republic authorities shall issue acts in order to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden, this constitution has been used as I think the basis for the opinion of Dr. Gow that this was an illustration, it was showing that Serbia was preparing for the dissolution of Yugoslavia. Would you agree with that opinion of Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what he meant by preparing for the dissolution of Yugoslavia. It certainly comes up in the context in which the constitutional order of Yugoslavia has been threatened, but not in this particular set of concerns by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So it was not Serbia but the other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Specifically Slovenia. May I draw your attention perhaps because it might be one of the relevant articles of this constitution, Article 135 of that constitution contained in Exhibit 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. It is Chapter 8 the relationship to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the first paragraph of Article 135 is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I cannot. As printed it does not make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- it is on the screen. So you do not 28 understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this sentence is meaningless to me, "The rights and duties vested under the present constitution in the Republic of Serbia which is part of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, violate the equal terms of the federal constitution are to be exercised in the federation." Grammatically it is wrong. It does not scan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then please provide you with the original text of Article 135. I tender the original text as an Exhibit, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, yes, this is a photocopy of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia in Serbian, dated Belgrade 1990, and Article 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to present to you a text which is supposed to be a translation of Article 135.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I have to get the original back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tender this document as well, your Honour, as Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 47 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to have ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me one minute, Mr. Orie. I was just thinking, Mr. Orie, I gather where you are going is that this witness, whoever translated it, will offer a different translation than what we received from the Prosecutor in Exhibit 24 for Article 135 which we will, if there is no objection, receive that. But we have encountered so many difficulties with 28 interpretation -- not so many but some -- we, perhaps, would want the Serbo-Croatian then to be put on the screen after we see this and have our interpreters translate it and then see among the three what we come up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You see, your Honour, there was no attention paid to Article 135 in the Prosecution's case, so that is the reason why we did not notice at that moment that on this part, in our view, the translation was incorrect. But I have some difficulties asking Professor Hayden questions about a part of an article that is totally un-understandable for him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand your point and 47 is admitted. Let us see what his translation is. I suppose I am just curious, if it does not take too much time, to see what we might get as a third. So here it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, clause 1: "The rights and duties that the Republic of Serbia which is within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has under this constitution and which by the federal constitution are realised within the federation will be realised in accordance with the federal constitution."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is clause 1, this is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is Serbo -- that is in Serbian? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I speak Serbo-Croatian but ......

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is there. I do not know that the interpreters have it. Can you read it well enough to interpret it? OK. Let us see. This is now the interpreters' translation 28 of Article 135 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 24 and we have the English translation in Defence Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The rights and duties of the Republic of Serbia being a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia enjoys under this constitution, and which are to be exercised at a federal level under the or according to the federal constitution shall be exercised" -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do we have the channel 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I now do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you could begin again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The rights and duties which the Republic of Serbia being a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia enjoys under this constitution and which pursuant to the federal constitution are exercised or enjoyed at the federal level, rather, in the federation, at the federal level, shall be exercised in conformity or in accordance with the federal constitution. "When acts of federal agencies or acts of agencies of another Republic in contravention to the rights and duties which that Republic which it has, which that Republic enjoys under the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia violate or infringe upon the quality of the Republic of Serbia", and we cannot see the rest of the text -- "infringe upon", whatever, "rights of the Republic of Serbia" -- I am sorry, I have forgotten -- "or threatens its interests, or infringes upon its interests in any other way without providing a compensation or indemnity for it, then the Republican agencies shall adopt 28 acts to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Hayden ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry. We were so interested, we just wanted to go on, but we will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 o'clock.
